'''漏刻博士'''（ろうこくはかせ）は、[[日本]][[律令制]]において[[陰陽寮]]に置かれた[[博士]]。[[和訓]]は「ときつかさ」。[[唐名]]は司辰・契壷司。定員2名で時には[[権官]]が置かれた。[[従七位下]]相当であるが、五位・六位が任じられた例もある（『[[職源鈔]]』）。
[[仕丁]]から選抜された[[守辰丁]]（20名）を率いて[[漏刻]]を警備するとともに、時刻を計り、定時に守辰丁に命じて陰陽寮内に設置された[[鐘]]を撃たせた。[[天皇]]の[[行幸]]の際には漏刻博士1名と守辰丁12名が漏刻とともに随従する義務があった。
もっとも、漏刻の技術は比較的早くに途絶えたとされ、[[院政]]期には[[賀茂氏]]・[[阿倍氏|阿倍氏]]の一員やその推挙する門人のための[[官職]]となる。[[菅野季親]]・[[菅野季長|季長]]は漏刻ではなく、[[年筮]]の達人として漏刻博士となったとされる。なお、[[大宰府]]・[[陸奥国]]（後に[[出羽国]]を追加）にも漏刻は設置されたが、博士は置かれずに守辰丁が管理していたとされている。
{{DEFAULTSORT:ろうこくはかせ}} [[Category:律令制の官制]] [[Category:陰陽道]] {{Japanese-history-stub}}

'''漏刻博士'''（ろうこくはかせ）は、[[日本]][[律令制]]において[[陰陽寮]]に置かれた[[博士]]。[[和訓]]は「ときつかさ」。[[唐名]]は司辰・契壷司。定員2名で時には[[権官]]が置かれた。[[従七位下]]相当であるが、五位・六位が任じられた例もある（『[[職源鈔]]』）。
[[仕丁]]から選抜された[[守辰丁]]（20名）を率いて[[漏刻]]を警備するとともに、時刻を計り、定時に守辰丁に命じて陰陽寮内に設置された[[鐘]]を打たせた。[[天皇]]の[[行幸]]の際には漏刻博士1名と守辰丁12名が漏刻とともに随従する義務があった。
なお、唐にも漏刻博士の官職は存在したが、唐では漏刻の実務は挈壺正・司辰・漏刻典事が行って漏刻博士は漏刻生を教育することが職掌とされていた。これに対して、日本では挈壺正・司辰・漏刻典事が設けられずに漏刻博士がその職掌を行い、反対に漏刻生の制度も設けられなかったために漏刻博士に教育の職掌が無かった（これは実務を行いながら、学生の教育も行った[[陰陽博士]]や[[天文博士]]、[[暦博士]]と異なる）<ref>木下正史『古代の漏刻と時刻制度』（吉川弘文館、2020年）ISBN 978-4-642-04657-2 P307-312.</ref>。
もっとも、漏刻の技術は比較的早くに途絶えたとされ、[[院政]]期には[[賀茂氏]]・[[阿倍氏|安倍氏]]の一員やその推挙する門人のための[[官職]]となる。[[菅野季親]]・[[菅野季長|季長]]は漏刻ではなく、[[年筮]]の達人として漏刻博士となったとされる。なお、[[大宰府]]・[[陸奥国]]（後に[[出羽国]]を追加）にも漏刻は設置されたが、博士は置かれずに守辰丁が管理していたとされている。

{{draft}} {{AFC comment|1=Note: This draft started from a complete copy of [[Onmyōji]] as it has a lot of redlinks with claims I want to keep. I will trim down into just the claim on an individual thing later[[User:Immanuelle|'''Immanuel'''le]] ❤️💚💙 [[User_talk:Immanuelle|(talk to the cutest Wikipedian)]] 01:41, 25 April 2023 (UTC)}} {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} is a topic related to [[Onmyodo]]
Later, [[Emperor Tenmu]] was such a master of astrology and fugue that he took his own divination tools and told fortunes during the [[Jinshin War]]. He also had a deep knowledge of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy, which led to the establishment of the Bureau of Onmyō and Japan's first [[observatory]] in 676, and the use of the term "onmyōji" in 685, which further increased the popularity of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy. In 718, the [[Yōrō Code]] established the Bureau of Onmyō as an internal department of the Ministry of Center, and when it was stipulated that the positions of {{ill|Temmon Hakase|lt=Doctor of Astrology|ja|天文博士}}, {{ill|Onmyō Hakase|lt=Doctor of Onmyō|ja|陰陽博士}}, onmyōji, {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}}, and {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} should be permanently assigned as technical officers, the Bureau of Onmyō became officially in charge of divination along with the [[turtle shell]] diviners who belonged to the [[Department of Divinities]].
==In media== === Books === * ''[[Teito Monogatari]]'', written by [[Hiroshi Aramata]], published in 1985 * ''[[Onmyōji (novel series)|Onmyōji]]'', written by [[Baku Yumemakura]], published in 1988 * ''[[The Summer of the Ubume]]'', ''[[Mōryō no Hako]]'' and other Kyōgokudō series, written by [[Natsuhiko Kyogoku]], published in 1994 * ''{{ill|Onmyō no Miyako|ja|陰陽ノ京}}'', written by [[Soichiro Watase]], published in 2001 * ''[[Shōnen Onmyōji]]'', written by [[Mitsuru Yūki]], published in 2001 * ''[[Rental Magica]]'', written by {{ill|Makoto Sanda|ja|三田誠}}, published in 2004 * ''{{ill|Bakemonogatari|ja|化物語}}'', written by [[Nisio Isin]], published in 2005 * ''[[Fairy Navigator Runa]]'', written by {{ill|Miyoko Ikeda|ja|池田美代子}}, published in 2008 * ''[[Tokyo Ravens]]'', written by {{ill|Kōhei Azano|ja|あざの耕平}}, published in 2010
=== Manga and anime ===
* ''[[Tokyo Babylon]]'', written by [[Clamp (manga artists)|Clamp]], published in 1990 * ''[[X (manga)|X]]'', written by Clamp, published in 1992 * ''[[Shaman King]]'', written by [[Hiroyuki Takei]], published in 1998 * ''[[Gag Manga Biyori]]'', written by [[Kōsuke Masuda]], published in 2000 * ''[[Magical Shopping Arcade Abenobashi]]'', created by [[Gainax]], published in 2001 * ''[[Amatsuki]]'', written by {{ill|Shinobu Takayama|ja|高山しのぶ}}, published in 2002 * ''[[Gin Tama]]'', written by [[Hideaki Sorachi]], published in 2003 * ''[[xxxHolic]]'', written by Clamp, published in 2003 * ''[[Onmyō Taisenki]]'', written by Yoshihiko Tomizawa, published in 2003 * ''[[Musashi Gundoh]]'', based on an unused story by [[Monkey Punch]], published in 2006 * ''{{ill|Shibariya Komachi|ja|縛り屋小町}}'', written by [[Mick Takeuchi]], published in 2006 * ''[[Nura: Rise of the Yokai Clan]]'', written by [[Hiroshi Shiibashi]], published in 2008 * ''[[Twin Star Exorcists]]'', written by {{ill|Yoshiaki Sukeno|ja|助野嘉昭}}, published in 2013 * ''[[The Reincarnation of the Strongest Exorcist in Another World |The Reincarnation of the Strongest Exorcist in Another World]]'', written by Kiichi Kosuzu, published in 2018 * ''[[MAO (manga)|MAO]]'', written by [[Rumiko Takahashi]], published in 2019
=== Films === *''[[Tokyo: The Last Megalopolis]]'', a 1988 Japanese fantasy film directed by [[Akio Jissōji]], based on the novel ''[[Teito Monogatari]]'' by Hiroshi Aramata *[[Onmyōji (film)|''Onmyōji'' (film)]], a 2001 Japanese film based on the [[Onmyōji (novel series)|''Onmyōji'' (novel series)]], by Baku Yumemakura and released in the U.S. in 2003 as ''Onmyōji - The Yin Yang Master'' **''[[Onmyōji 2]]'', the 2003 sequel *''[[The Yin-Yang Master: Dream of Eternity]]'', a 2020 Chinese fantasy film based on the [[Onmyōji (novel series)|''Onmyōji'' (novel series)]], by Baku Yumemakura directed by [[Guo Jingming]], and starring [[Mark Chao]] and [[Deng Lun]] *''[[The Yinyang Master]]'', a 2021 Chinese fantasy film directed by Li Weiran, and starring [[Chen Kun]], [[Zhou Xun]] and [[William Chan]] based on the game that was based on the [[Onmyōji (novel series)|''Onmyōji'' (novel series)]], by Baku Yumemakura
=== Video games === * ''{{ill|Kuon no Kizuna|ja|久遠の絆}}'', developed by [[FOG Inc.]], released in 1998 * ''[[Tokyo Majin Gakuen]]'', produced by {{ill|Shūhō Imai|ja|今井秋芳}}, released in 1998 * ''[[Kuon]]'', developed by [[FromSoftware]], released in 2004 * ''[[11eyes: Tsumi to Batsu to Aganai no Shōjo]]'', developed by {{ill|Lass (video game developer)|lt=Lass|ja|Lass}}, released in 2008 * ''[[Naraka: Bladepoint]]'', developed by [[24 Entertainment]], released in 2021 features the character [[Kurumi Tsuchimikado]], who according to game lore is the first female Onmyōji, descended from a long line of Onmyōdō masters.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.narakathegame.com/index.html|title = Naraka: Bladepoint - New Hero Out Now!}}</ref>

revision.text:
{{draft}} {{AFC comment|1=Note: This draft started from a complete copy of [[Onmyōji]] as it has a lot of redlinks with claims I want to keep. I will trim down into just the claim on an individual thing later[[User:Immanuelle|'''Immanuel'''le]] ❤️💚💙 [[User_talk:Immanuelle|(talk to the cutest Wikipedian)]] 01:41, 25 April 2023 (UTC)}} {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} is position in the [[Ministry of the Center]] the chief timekeeper.<ref name="titsingh427">Titsingh, Isaac. (1834). {{Google books|18oNAAAAIAAJ|''Annales des empereurs du japon,'' p. 427.|page=427}}</ref><ref>https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/10.7916/d8-3zya-0s65/download</ref><ref>https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/10.7916/D8HD82PN/download</ref><ref>https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/id=8943</ref><ref>https://bazhum.muzhp.pl/media/files/Analecta_Nipponica/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1-s139-202/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1-s139-202.pdf</ref>
Later, [[Emperor Tenmu]] was such a master of astrology and fugue that he took his own divination tools and told fortunes during the [[Jinshin War]]. He also had a deep knowledge of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy, which led to the establishment of the Bureau of Onmyō and Japan's first [[observatory]] in 676, and the use of the term "onmyōji" in 685, which further increased the popularity of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy. In 718, the [[Yōrō Code]] established the Bureau of Onmyō as an internal department of the Ministry of Center, and when it was stipulated that the positions of {{ill|Temmon Hakase|lt=Doctor of Astrology|ja|天文博士}}, {{ill|Onmyō Hakase|lt=Doctor of Onmyō|ja|陰陽博士}}, onmyōji, {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}}, and {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} should be permanently assigned as technical officers, the Bureau of Onmyō became officially in charge of divination along with the [[turtle shell]] diviners who belonged to the [[Department of Divinities]].
==In media== === Books === * ''[[Teito Monogatari]]'', written by [[Hiroshi Aramata]], published in 1985 * ''[[Onmyōji (novel series)|Onmyōji]]'', written by [[Baku Yumemakura]], published in 1988 * ''[[The Summer of the Ubume]]'', ''[[Mōryō no Hako]]'' and other Kyōgokudō series, written by [[Natsuhiko Kyogoku]], published in 1994 * ''{{ill|Onmyō no Miyako|ja|陰陽ノ京}}'', written by [[Soichiro Watase]], published in 2001 * ''[[Shōnen Onmyōji]]'', written by [[Mitsuru Yūki]], published in 2001 * ''[[Rental Magica]]'', written by {{ill|Makoto Sanda|ja|三田誠}}, published in 2004 * ''{{ill|Bakemonogatari|ja|化物語}}'', written by [[Nisio Isin]], published in 2005 * ''[[Fairy Navigator Runa]]'', written by {{ill|Miyoko Ikeda|ja|池田美代子}}, published in 2008 * ''[[Tokyo Ravens]]'', written by {{ill|Kōhei Azano|ja|あざの耕平}}, published in 2010
=== Manga and anime ===
* ''[[Tokyo Babylon]]'', written by [[Clamp (manga artists)|Clamp]], published in 1990 * ''[[X (manga)|X]]'', written by Clamp, published in 1992 * ''[[Shaman King]]'', written by [[Hiroyuki Takei]], published in 1998 * ''[[Gag Manga Biyori]]'', written by [[Kōsuke Masuda]], published in 2000 * ''[[Magical Shopping Arcade Abenobashi]]'', created by [[Gainax]], published in 2001 * ''[[Amatsuki]]'', written by {{ill|Shinobu Takayama|ja|高山しのぶ}}, published in 2002 * ''[[Gin Tama]]'', written by [[Hideaki Sorachi]], published in 2003 * ''[[xxxHolic]]'', written by Clamp, published in 2003 * ''[[Onmyō Taisenki]]'', written by Yoshihiko Tomizawa, published in 2003 * ''[[Musashi Gundoh]]'', based on an unused story by [[Monkey Punch]], published in 2006 * ''{{ill|Shibariya Komachi|ja|縛り屋小町}}'', written by [[Mick Takeuchi]], published in 2006 * ''[[Nura: Rise of the Yokai Clan]]'', written by [[Hiroshi Shiibashi]], published in 2008 * ''[[Twin Star Exorcists]]'', written by {{ill|Yoshiaki Sukeno|ja|助野嘉昭}}, published in 2013 * ''[[The Reincarnation of the Strongest Exorcist in Another World]]'', written by Kiichi Kosuzu, published in 2018 * ''[[MAO (manga)|MAO]]'', written by [[Rumiko Takahashi]], published in 2019
=== Films === *''[[Tokyo: The Last Megalopolis]]'', a 1988 Japanese fantasy film directed by [[Akio Jissōji]], based on the novel ''[[Teito Monogatari]]'' by Hiroshi Aramata *[[Onmyōji (film)|''Onmyōji'' (film)]], a 2001 Japanese film based on the [[Onmyōji (novel series)|''Onmyōji'' (novel series)]], by Baku Yumemakura and released in the U.S. in 2003 as ''Onmyōji - The Yin Yang Master'' **''[[Onmyōji 2]]'', the 2003 sequel *''[[The Yin-Yang Master: Dream of Eternity]]'', a 2020 Chinese fantasy film based on the [[Onmyōji (novel series)|''Onmyōji'' (novel series)]], by Baku Yumemakura directed by [[Guo Jingming]], and starring [[Mark Chao]] and [[Deng Lun]] *''[[The Yinyang Master]]'', a 2021 Chinese fantasy film directed by Li Weiran, and starring [[Chen Kun]], [[Zhou Xun]] and [[William Chan]] based on the game that was based on the [[Onmyōji (novel series)|''Onmyōji'' (novel series)]], by Baku Yumemakura
=== Video games === * ''{{ill|Kuon no Kizuna|ja|久遠の絆}}'', developed by [[FOG Inc.]], released in 1998 * ''[[Tokyo Majin Gakuen]]'', produced by {{ill|Shūhō Imai|ja|今井秋芳}}, released in 1998 * ''[[Kuon]]'', developed by [[FromSoftware]], released in 2004 * ''[[11eyes: Tsumi to Batsu to Aganai no Shōjo]]'', developed by {{ill|Lass (video game developer)|lt=Lass|ja|Lass}}, released in 2008 * ''[[Naraka: Bladepoint]]'', developed by [[24 Entertainment]], released in 2021 features the character [[Kurumi Tsuchimikado]], who according to game lore is the first female Onmyōji, descended from a long line of Onmyōdō masters.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.narakathegame.com/index.html|title = Naraka: Bladepoint - New Hero Out Now!}}</ref>
== See also ==
* [[Abe no Seimei]] * [[Da Liu Ren]] * [[Goryō]] * [[Itako]] * [[Kuji-in]] * [[Onmyōdō]] * [[Sanpaku]] * [[Seimei Shrine]] * [[Senji Ryakketsu]] * [[Shikigami]] * [[Shinigami]] * [[Tengenjutsu (fortune telling)]] * [[Ushi no toki mairi]]

{{draft}} {{AFC comment|1=Note: This draft started from a complete copy of [[Onmyōji]] as it has a lot of redlinks with claims I want to keep. I will trim down into just the claim on an individual thing later[[User:Immanuelle|'''Immanuel'''le]] ❤️💚💙 [[User_talk:Immanuelle|(talk to the cutest Wikipedian)]] 01:41, 25 April 2023 (UTC)}} {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} is position in the [[Ministry of the Center]] the chief timekeeper.<ref name="titsingh427">Titsingh, Isaac. (1834). {{Google books|18oNAAAAIAAJ|''Annales des empereurs du japon,'' p. 427.|page=427}}</ref><ref>https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/10.7916/d8-3zya-0s65/download</ref><ref>https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/10.7916/D8HD82PN/download</ref><ref>https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/id=8943</ref><ref>https://bazhum.muzhp.pl/media/files/Analecta_Nipponica/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1-s139-202/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1-s139-202.pdf</ref>
Later, [[Emperor Tenmu]] was such a master of astrology and fugue that he took his own divination tools and told fortunes during the [[Jinshin War]]. He also had a deep knowledge of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy, which led to the establishment of the Bureau of Onmyō and Japan's first [[observatory]] in 676, and the use of the term "onmyōji" in 685, which further increased the popularity of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy. In 718, the [[Yōrō Code]] established the Bureau of Onmyō as an internal department of the Ministry of Center, and when it was stipulated that the positions of {{ill|Temmon Hakase|lt=Doctor of Astrology|ja|天文博士}}, {{ill|Onmyō Hakase|lt=Doctor of Onmyō|ja|陰陽博士}}, onmyōji, {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}}, and {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} should be permanently assigned as technical officers, the Bureau of Onmyō became officially in charge of divination along with the [[turtle shell]] diviners who belonged to the [[Department of Divinities]].
==In media== === Books === * ''[[Teito Monogatari]]'', written by [[Hiroshi Aramata]], published in 1985 * ''[[Onmyōji (novel series)|Onmyōji]]'', written by [[Baku Yumemakura]], published in 1988 * ''[[The Summer of the Ubume]]'', ''[[Mōryō no Hako]]'' and other Kyōgokudō series, written by [[Natsuhiko Kyogoku]], published in 1994 * ''{{ill|Onmyō no Miyako|ja|陰陽ノ京}}'', written by [[Soichiro Watase]], published in 2001 * ''[[Shōnen Onmyōji]]'', written by [[Mitsuru Yūki]], published in 2001 * ''[[Rental Magica]]'', written by {{ill|Makoto Sanda|ja|三田誠}}, published in 2004 * ''{{ill|Bakemonogatari|ja|化物語}}'', written by [[Nisio Isin]], published in 2005 * ''[[Fairy Navigator Runa]]'', written by {{ill|Miyoko Ikeda|ja|池田美代子}}, published in 2008 * ''[[Tokyo Ravens]]'', written by {{ill|Kōhei Azano|ja|あざの耕平}}, published in 2010
=== Manga and anime ===
* ''[[Tokyo Babylon]]'', written by [[Clamp (manga artists)|Clamp]], published in 1990 * ''[[X (manga)|X]]'', written by Clamp, published in 1992 * ''[[Shaman King]]'', written by [[Hiroyuki Takei]], published in 1998 * ''[[Gag Manga Biyori]]'', written by [[Kōsuke Masuda]], published in 2000 * ''[[Magical Shopping Arcade Abenobashi]]'', created by [[Gainax]], published in 2001 * ''[[Amatsuki]]'', written by {{ill|Shinobu Takayama|ja|高山しのぶ}}, published in 2002 * ''[[Gin Tama]]'', written by [[Hideaki Sorachi]], published in 2003 * ''[[xxxHolic]]'', written by Clamp, published in 2003 * ''[[Onmyō Taisenki]]'', written by Yoshihiko Tomizawa, published in 2003 * ''[[Musashi Gundoh]]'', based on an unused story by [[Monkey Punch]], published in 2006 * ''{{ill|Shibariya Komachi|ja|縛り屋小町}}'', written by [[Mick Takeuchi]], published in 2006 * ''[[Nura: Rise of the Yokai Clan]]'', written by [[Hiroshi Shiibashi]], published in 2008 * ''[[Twin Star Exorcists]]'', written by {{ill|Yoshiaki Sukeno|ja|助野嘉昭}}, published in 2013 * ''[[The Reincarnation of the Strongest Exorcist in Another World]]'', written by Kiichi Kosuzu, published in 2018 * ''[[MAO (manga)|MAO]]'', written by [[Rumiko Takahashi]], published in 2019
=== Films === *''[[Tokyo: The Last Megalopolis]]'', a 1988 Japanese fantasy film directed by [[Akio Jissōji]], based on the novel ''[[Teito Monogatari]]'' by Hiroshi Aramata *[[Onmyōji (film)|''Onmyōji'' (film)]], a 2001 Japanese film based on the [[Onmyōji (novel series)|''Onmyōji'' (novel series)]], by Baku Yumemakura and released in the U.S. in 2003 as ''Onmyōji - The Yin Yang Master'' **''[[Onmyōji 2]]'', the 2003 sequel *''[[The Yin-Yang Master: Dream of Eternity]]'', a 2020 Chinese fantasy film based on the [[Onmyōji (novel series)|''Onmyōji'' (novel series)]], by Baku Yumemakura directed by [[Guo Jingming]], and starring [[Mark Chao]] and [[Deng Lun]] *''[[The Yinyang Master]]'', a 2021 Chinese fantasy film directed by Li Weiran, and starring [[Chen Kun]], [[Zhou Xun]] and [[William Chan]] based on the game that was based on the [[Onmyōji (novel series)|''Onmyōji'' (novel series)]], by Baku Yumemakura
=== Video games === * ''{{ill|Kuon no Kizuna|ja|久遠の絆}}'', developed by [[FOG Inc.]], released in 1998 * ''[[Tokyo Majin Gakuen]]'', produced by {{ill|Shūhō Imai|ja|今井秋芳}}, released in 1998 * ''[[Kuon]]'', developed by [[FromSoftware]], released in 2004 * ''[[11eyes: Tsumi to Batsu to Aganai no Shōjo]]'', developed by {{ill|Lass (video game developer)|lt=Lass|ja|Lass}}, released in 2008 * ''[[Naraka: Bladepoint]]'', developed by [[24 Entertainment]], released in 2021 features the character [[Kurumi Tsuchimikado]], who according to game lore is the first female Onmyōji, descended from a long line of Onmyōdō masters.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.narakathegame.com/index.html|title = Naraka: Bladepoint - New Hero Out Now!}}</ref>

{{draft}} {{AFC comment|1=Note: This draft started from a complete copy of [[Onmyōji]] as it has a lot of redlinks with claims I want to keep. I will trim down into just the claim on an individual thing later[[User:Immanuelle|'''Immanuel'''le]] ❤️💚💙 [[User_talk:Immanuelle|(talk to the cutest Wikipedian)]] 01:41, 25 April 2023 (UTC)}} {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} (Rōkoku Hakase, 漏刻博士) is position in the [[Ministry of the Center]] the chief timekeeper.<ref name="titsingh427">Titsingh, Isaac. (1834). {{Google books|18oNAAAAIAAJ|''Annales des empereurs du japon,'' p. 427.|page=427}}</ref><ref>https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/10.7916/d8-3zya-0s65/download</ref><ref>https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/10.7916/D8HD82PN/download</ref><ref>https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/id=8943</ref><ref>https://bazhum.muzhp.pl/media/files/Analecta_Nipponica/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1-s139-202/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1-s139-202.pdf</ref>
The position was a {{ill|Hakase|ja|博士 (文官)}} under the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制}} within the {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}}. The {{ill|Japanese reading|ja|和訓}} (和訓) for this position was "Tokitsukasa" (ときつかさ), while its {{ill|Chinese name|ja|唐名}} was "Shijin" (司辰) or "Keiko-shi" (契壷司). Two individuals typically filled this role, though additional deputy officials ({{ill|Gonkan|ja|権官}}) were occasionally appointed. Officially classified as {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Lower Grade|ja|従七位下}}, individuals of higher ranks, such as the fifth or sixth ranks, were sometimes appointed to this position (as noted in the {{ill|Shokugenshō|ja|職源鈔}}). [[ja:漏刻博士]] The Rōkoku Hakase supervised the {{ill|Morishin-chō|ja|守辰丁}}, a group of 20 individuals selected from {{ill|Shichō|ja|仕丁}}, who guarded the {{ill|Water clocks|ja|漏刻}} and operated them to measure time. At designated times, they would order the Morishin-chō to strike the {{ill|bells|ja|鐘}} located within the Onmyōryō. During the [[Emperor of Japan|Emperor]]'s {{ill|Imperial visits|ja|行幸}}, one Rōkoku Hakase and twelve Morishin-chō were required to accompany the water clock.
In {{ill|Tang dynasty|ja|唐}}, a similar role for a Rōkoku Hakase existed, but the responsibilities were distinct. In Tang China, the practical tasks of water clocks were managed by officials such as Kekkosei (挈壺正), Shijin (司辰), and Rokoku Tenshi (漏刻典事), while the Rōkoku Hakase focused on teaching students of water clocks (Rokokusei). Conversely, in Japan, the practical roles of Kekkosei and related officials were incorporated into the duties of the Rōkoku Hakase. Japan did not establish a Rokokusei system, meaning that Rōkoku Hakase did not have educational duties. This contrasts with the roles of {{ill|Tenmon Hakase|ja|天文博士}} (Astronomy Doctor) and {{ill|Reki Hakase|ja|暦博士}} (Calendar Doctor), who both managed practical tasks and taught students.<ref>Masashi Kinoshita, ''Kodai no Rōkoku to Jikoku Seido'' (Ancient Water Clocks and Time Systems), Yoshikawa Kōbunkan, 2020, ISBN 978-4-642-04657-2, pp. 307–312.</ref>
The water clock system appears to have declined relatively early. By the {{ill|Insei|ja|院政}} period, the role of Rōkoku Hakase became symbolic, primarily awarded to members of the {{ill|Kamo clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} or {{ill|Abe clan|ja|阿倍氏}} or their recommended disciples. Figures such as {{ill|Sugano no Suketaka|ja|菅野季親}} and {{ill|Sugano no Suketaka|ja|菅野季長}} became Rōkoku Hakase not for expertise in water clocks but for their skill in annual divination ({{ill|Nensei|ja|年筮}}). Although water clocks were also installed in {{ill|Dazaifu|ja|大宰府}} and {{ill|Mutsu Province|ja|陸奥国}} (and later in {{ill|Dewa Province|ja|出羽国}}), they were managed solely by Morishin-chō without a corresponding Hakase.
== History == Later, [[Emperor Tenmu]] was such a master of astrology and fugue that he took his own divination tools and told fortunes during the [[Jinshin War]]. He also had a deep knowledge of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy, which led to the establishment of the Bureau of Onmyō and Japan's first [[observatory]] in 676, and the use of the term "onmyōji" in 685, which further increased the popularity of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy. In 718, the [[Yōrō Code]] established the Bureau of Onmyō as an internal department of the Ministry of Center, and when it was stipulated that the positions of {{ill|Temmon Hakase|lt=Doctor of Astrology|ja|天文博士}}, {{ill|Onmyō Hakase|lt=Doctor of Onmyō|ja|陰陽博士}}, onmyōji, {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}}, and {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} should be permanently assigned as technical officers, the Bureau of Onmyō became officially in charge of divination along with the [[turtle shell]] diviners who belonged to the [[Department of Divinities]].

{{draft}} {{AFC comment|1=Note: This draft started from a complete copy of [[Onmyōji]] as it has a lot of redlinks with claims I want to keep. I will trim down into just the claim on an individual thing later[[User:Immanuelle|'''Immanuel'''le]] ❤️💚💙 [[User_talk:Immanuelle|(talk to the cutest Wikipedian)]] 01:41, 25 April 2023 (UTC)}} {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} (Rōkoku Hakase, 漏刻博士) is position in the [[Ministry of the Center]] the chief timekeeper.<ref name="titsingh427">Titsingh, Isaac. (1834). {{Google books|18oNAAAAIAAJ|''Annales des empereurs du japon,'' p. 427.|page=427}}</ref><ref>https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/10.7916/d8-3zya-0s65/download</ref><ref>https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/10.7916/D8HD82PN/download</ref><ref>https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/id=8943</ref><ref>https://bazhum.muzhp.pl/media/files/Analecta_Nipponica/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1-s139-202/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1-s139-202.pdf</ref>
The position was a {{ill|Hakase|ja|博士 (文官)}} under the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制}} within the {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}}. The {{ill|Japanese reading|ja|和訓}} (和訓) for this position was "Tokitsukasa" (ときつかさ), while its {{ill|Chinese name|ja|唐名}} was "Shijin" (司辰) or "Keiko-shi" (契壷司). Two individuals typically filled this role, though additional deputy officials ({{ill|Gonkan|ja|権官}}) were occasionally appointed. Officially classified as {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Lower Grade|ja|従七位下}}, individuals of higher ranks, such as the fifth or sixth ranks, were sometimes appointed to this position (as noted in the {{ill|Shokugenshō|ja|職源鈔}}). [[Category:dd]][[ja:漏刻博士]] The Rōkoku Hakase supervised the {{ill|Morishin-chō|ja|守辰丁}}, a group of 20 individuals selected from {{ill|Shichō|ja|仕丁}}, who guarded the {{ill|Water clocks|ja|漏刻}} and operated them to measure time. At designated times, they would order the Morishin-chō to strike the {{ill|bells|ja|鐘}} located within the Onmyōryō. During the [[Emperor of Japan|Emperor]]'s {{ill|Imperial visits|ja|行幸}}, one Rōkoku Hakase and twelve Morishin-chō were required to accompany the water clock.
In {{ill|Tang dynasty|ja|唐}}, a similar role for a Rōkoku Hakase existed, but the responsibilities were distinct. In Tang China, the practical tasks of water clocks were managed by officials such as Kekkosei (挈壺正), Shijin (司辰), and Rokoku Tenshi (漏刻典事), while the Rōkoku Hakase focused on teaching students of water clocks (Rokokusei). Conversely, in Japan, the practical roles of Kekkosei and related officials were incorporated into the duties of the Rōkoku Hakase. Japan did not establish a Rokokusei system, meaning that Rōkoku Hakase did not have educational duties. This contrasts with the roles of {{ill|Tenmon Hakase|ja|天文博士}} (Astronomy Doctor) and {{ill|Reki Hakase|ja|暦博士}} (Calendar Doctor), who both managed practical tasks and taught students.<ref>Masashi Kinoshita, ''Kodai no Rōkoku to Jikoku Seido'' (Ancient Water Clocks and Time Systems), Yoshikawa Kōbunkan, 2020, ISBN 978-4-642-04657-2, pp. 307–312.</ref>
The water clock system appears to have declined relatively early. By the {{ill|Insei|ja|院政}} period, the role of Rōkoku Hakase became symbolic, primarily awarded to members of the {{ill|Kamo clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} or {{ill|Abe clan|ja|阿倍氏}} or their recommended disciples. Figures such as {{ill|Sugano no Suketaka|ja|菅野季親}} and {{ill|Sugano no Suketaka|ja|菅野季長}} became Rōkoku Hakase not for expertise in water clocks but for their skill in annual divination ({{ill|Nensei|ja|年筮}}). Although water clocks were also installed in {{ill|Dazaifu|ja|大宰府}} and {{ill|Mutsu Province|ja|陸奥国}} (and later in {{ill|Dewa Province|ja|出羽国}}), they were managed solely by Morishin-chō without a corresponding Hakase.
== History == Later, [[Emperor Tenmu]] was such a master of astrology and fugue that he took his own divination tools and told fortunes during the [[Jinshin War]]. He also had a deep knowledge of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy, which led to the establishment of the Bureau of Onmyō and Japan's first [[observatory]] in 676, and the use of the term "onmyōji" in 685, which further increased the popularity of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy. In 718, the [[Yōrō Code]] established the Bureau of Onmyō as an internal department of the Ministry of Center, and when it was stipulated that the positions of {{ill|Temmon Hakase|lt=Doctor of Astrology|ja|天文博士}}, {{ill|Onmyō Hakase|lt=Doctor of Onmyō|ja|陰陽博士}}, onmyōji, {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}}, and {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} should be permanently assigned as technical officers, the Bureau of Onmyō became officially in charge of divination along with the [[turtle shell]] diviners who belonged to the [[Department of Divinities]].

In Tang China, the practical tasks of water clocks were managed by officials such as Kekkosei (挈壺正), Shijin (司辰), and Rokoku Tenshi (漏刻典事), while the Rōkoku Hakase focused on teaching students of water clocks (Rokokusei). Conversely, in Japan, the practical roles of Kekkosei and related officials were incorporated into the duties of the Rōkoku Hakase. Japan did not establish a Rokokusei system, meaning that Rōkoku Hakase did not have educational duties. This contrasts with the roles of {{ill|Tenmon Hakase|ja|天文博士}} (Astronomy Doctor) and {{ill|Reki Hakase|ja|暦博士}} (Calendar Doctor), who both managed practical tasks and taught students.<ref>Masashi Kinoshita, ''Kodai no Rōkoku to Jikoku Seido'' (Ancient Water Clocks and Time Systems), Yoshikawa Kōbunkan, 2020, ISBN 978-4-642-04657-2, pp. 307–312.</ref>
The water clock system appears to have declined relatively early. By the {{ill|Insei|ja|院政}} period, the role of Rōkoku Hakase became symbolic, primarily awarded to members of the {{ill|Kamo clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} or {{ill|Abe clan|ja|阿倍氏}} or their recommended disciples. Figures such as {{ill|Sugano no Suketaka|ja|菅野季親}} and {{ill|Sugano no Suketaka|ja|菅野季長}} became Rōkoku Hakase not for expertise in water clocks but for their skill in annual divination ({{ill|Nensei|ja|年筮}}). Although water clocks were also installed in {{ill|Dazaifu|ja|大宰府}} and {{ill|Mutsu Province|ja|陸奥国}} (and later in {{ill|Dewa Province|ja|出羽国}}), they were managed solely by Morishin-chō without a corresponding Hakase.
== History == Later, [[Emperor Tenmu]] was such a master of astrology and fugue that he took his own divination tools and told fortunes during the [[Jinshin War]]. He also had a deep knowledge of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy, which led to the establishment of the Bureau of Onmyō and Japan's first [[observatory]] in 676, and the use of the term "onmyōji" in 685, which further increased the popularity of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy. In 718, the [[Yōrō Code]] established the Bureau of Onmyō as an internal department of the Ministry of Center, and when it was stipulated that the positions of {{ill|Temmon Hakase|lt=Doctor of Astrology|ja|天文博士}}, {{ill|Onmyō Hakase|lt=Doctor of Onmyō|ja|陰陽博士}}, onmyōji, {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}}, and {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} should be permanently assigned as technical officers, the Bureau of Onmyō became officially in charge of divination along with the [[turtle shell]] diviners who belonged to the [[Department of Divinities]].

Two individuals typically filled this role, though additional deputy officials ({{ill|Gonkan|ja|権官}}) were occasionally appointed. Officially classified as {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Lower Grade|ja|従七位下}}, individuals of higher ranks, such as the fifth or sixth ranks, were sometimes appointed to this position (as noted in the {{ill|Shokugenshō|ja|職源鈔}}). At designated times, they would order the Morishin-chō to strike the {{ill|bells|ja|鐘}} located within the Onmyōryō. The water clock system appears to have declined relatively early. By the {{ill|Insei|ja|院政}} period, the role of Rōkoku Hakase became symbolic, primarily awarded to members of the {{ill|Kamo clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} or {{ill|Abe clan|ja|阿倍氏}} or their recommended disciples. Figures such as {{ill|Sugano no Suketaka|ja|菅野季親}} and {{ill|Sugano no Suketaka|ja|菅野季長}} became Rōkoku Hakase not for expertise in water clocks but for their skill in annual divination ({{ill|Nensei|ja|年筮}}). Although water clocks were also installed in {{ill|Dazaifu|ja|大宰府}} and {{ill|Mutsu Province|ja|陸奥国}} (and later in {{ill|Dewa Province|ja|出羽国}}), they were managed solely by Morishin-chō without a corresponding Hakase.

I will trim down into just the claim on an individual thing later[[User:Immanuelle|'''Immanuel'''le]] ❤️💚💙 [[User_talk:Immanuelle|(talk to the cutest Wikipedian)]] 01:41, 25 April 2023 (UTC)}} {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} (Rōkoku Hakase, 漏刻博士) is position in the [[Ministry of the Center]] the chief timekeeper.<ref name="titsingh427">Titsingh, Isaac. (1834). {{Google books|18oNAAAAIAAJ|''Annales des empereurs du japon,'' p. 427.|page=427}}</ref><ref>https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/10.7916/d8-3zya-0s65/download</ref><ref>https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/10.7916/D8HD82PN/download</ref><ref>https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/id=8943</ref><ref>https://bazhum.muzhp.pl/media/files/Analecta_Nipponica/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1-s139-202/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1-s139-202.pdf</ref>
The position was a {{ill|Hakase|ja|博士 (文官)}} under the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制}} within the {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}}. The {{ill|Japanese reading|ja|和訓}} (和訓) for this position was "Tokitsukasa" (ときつかさ), while its {{ill|Chinese name|ja|唐名}} was "Shijin" (司辰) or "Keiko-shi" (契壷司). Two individuals typically filled this role, though additional deputy officials ({{ill|Gonkan|ja|権官}}) were occasionally appointed. Officially classified as {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Lower Grade|ja|従七位下}}, individuals of higher ranks, such as the fifth or sixth ranks, were sometimes appointed to this position (as noted in the {{ill|Shokugenshō|ja|職源鈔}}). [[Category:dd]][[ja:漏刻博士]] The Rōkoku Hakase supervised the {{ill|Morishin-chō|ja|守辰丁}}, a group of 20 individuals selected from {{ill|Shichō|ja|仕丁}}, who guarded the {{ill|Water clocks|ja|漏刻}} and operated them to measure time. At designated times, they would order the Morishin-chō to strike the {{ill|bells|ja|鐘}} located within the Onmyōryō. During the [[Emperor of Japan|Emperor]]'s {{ill|Imperial visits|ja|行幸}}, one Rōkoku Hakase and twelve Morishin-chō were required to accompany the water clock.
In {{ill|Tang dynasty|ja|唐}}, a similar role for a Rōkoku Hakase existed, but the responsibilities were distinct. In Tang China, the practical tasks of water clocks were managed by officials such as Kekkosei (挈壺正), Shijin (司辰), and Rokoku Tenshi (漏刻典事), while the Rōkoku Hakase focused on teaching students of water clocks (Rokokusei). Conversely, in Japan, the practical roles of Kekkosei and related officials were incorporated into the duties of the Rōkoku Hakase. Japan did not establish a Rokokusei system, meaning that Rōkoku Hakase did not have educational duties. This contrasts with the roles of {{ill|Tenmon Hakase|ja|天文博士}} (Astronomy Doctor) and {{ill|Reki Hakase|ja|暦博士}} (Calendar Doctor), who both managed practical tasks and taught students.<ref>Masashi Kinoshita, ''Kodai no Rōkoku to Jikoku Seido'' (Ancient Water Clocks and Time Systems), Yoshikawa Kōbunkan, 2020, ISBN 978-4-642-04657-2, pp. 307–312.</ref>
The water clock system appears to have declined relatively early. By the {{ill|Insei|ja|院政}} period, the role of Rōkoku Hakase became symbolic, primarily awarded to members of the {{ill|Kamo clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} or {{ill|Abe clan|ja|阿倍氏}} or their recommended disciples. Figures such as {{ill|Sugano no Suketaka|ja|菅野季親}} and {{ill|Sugano no Suketaka|ja|菅野季長}} became Rōkoku Hakase not for expertise in water clocks but for their skill in annual divination ({{ill|Nensei|ja|年筮}}). Although water clocks were also installed in {{ill|Dazaifu|ja|大宰府}} and {{ill|Mutsu Province|ja|陸奥国}} (and later in {{ill|Dewa Province|ja|出羽国}}), they were managed solely by Morishin-chō without a corresponding Hakase.
== History == Later, [[Emperor Tenmu]] was such a master of astrology and fugue that he took his own divination tools and told fortunes during the [[Jinshin War]]. He also had a deep knowledge of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy, which led to the establishment of the Bureau of Onmyō and Japan's first [[observatory]] in 676, and the use of the term "onmyōji" in 685, which further increased the popularity of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy. In 718, the [[Yōrō Code]] established the Bureau of Onmyō as an internal department of the Ministry of Center, and when it was stipulated that the positions of {{ill|Temmon Hakase|lt=Doctor of Astrology|ja|天文博士}}, {{ill|Onmyō Hakase|lt=Doctor of Onmyō|ja|陰陽博士}}, onmyōji, {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}}, and {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} should be permanently assigned as technical officers, the Bureau of Onmyō became officially in charge of divination along with the [[turtle shell]] diviners who belonged to the [[Department of Divinities]].
== Related Articles == * {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制}} * {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}} * {{ill|Water clock|ja|漏刻}}

{{draft}} {{AFC comment|1=Note: This draft started from a complete copy of [[Onmyōji]] as it has a lot of redlinks with claims I want to keep. I will trim down into just the claim on an individual thing later[[User:Immanuelle|'''Immanuel'''le]] ❤️💚💙 [[User_talk:Immanuelle|(talk to the cutest Wikipedian)]] 01:41, 25 April 2023 (UTC)}} {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} (Rōkoku Hakase, 漏刻博士) is position in the [[Ministry of the Center]] the chief timekeeper.<ref name="titsingh427">Titsingh, Isaac. (1834). {{Google books|18oNAAAAIAAJ|''Annales des empereurs du japon,'' p. 427.|page=427}}</ref><ref>https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/10.7916/d8-3zya-0s65/download</ref><ref>https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/10.7916/D8HD82PN/download</ref><ref>https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/id=8943</ref><ref>https://bazhum.muzhp.pl/media/files/Analecta_Nipponica/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1-s139-202/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1-s139-202.pdf</ref>
The position was a {{ill|Hakase|ja|博士 (文官)}} under the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制}} within the {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}}. The {{ill|Japanese reading|ja|和訓}} (和訓) for this position was "Tokitsukasa" (ときつかさ), while its {{ill|Chinese name|ja|唐名}} was "Shijin" (司辰) or "Keiko-shi" (契壷司). Two individuals typically filled this role, though additional deputy officials ({{ill|Gonkan|ja|権官}}) were occasionally appointed. Officially classified as {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Lower Grade|ja|従七位下}}, individuals of higher ranks, such as the fifth or sixth ranks, were sometimes appointed to this position (as noted in the {{ill|Shokugenshō|ja|職源鈔}}). [[ja:漏刻博士]] The Rōkoku Hakase supervised the {{ill|Morishin-chō|ja|守辰丁}}, a group of 20 individuals selected from {{ill|Shichō|ja|仕丁}}, who guarded the {{ill|Water clocks|ja|漏刻}} and operated them to measure time. At designated times, they would order the Morishin-chō to strike the {{ill|bells|ja|鐘}} located within the Onmyōryō. During the [[Emperor of Japan|Emperor]]'s {{ill|Imperial visits|ja|行幸}}, one Rōkoku Hakase and twelve Morishin-chō were required to accompany the water clock.
In {{ill|Tang dynasty|ja|唐}}, a similar role for a Rōkoku Hakase existed, but the responsibilities were distinct. In Tang China, the practical tasks of water clocks were managed by officials such as Kekkosei (挈壺正), Shijin (司辰), and Rokoku Tenshi (漏刻典事), while the Rōkoku Hakase focused on teaching students of water clocks (Rokokusei). Conversely, in Japan, the practical roles of Kekkosei and related officials were incorporated into the duties of the Rōkoku Hakase. Japan did not establish a Rokokusei system, meaning that Rōkoku Hakase did not have educational duties. This contrasts with the roles of {{ill|Tenmon Hakase|ja|天文博士}} (Astronomy Doctor) and {{ill|Reki Hakase|ja|暦博士}} (Calendar Doctor), who both managed practical tasks and taught students.<ref>Masashi Kinoshita, ''Kodai no Rōkoku to Jikoku Seido'' (Ancient Water Clocks and Time Systems), Yoshikawa Kōbunkan, 2020, ISBN 978-4-642-04657-2, pp. 307–312.</ref>
The water clock system appears to have declined relatively early. By the {{ill|Insei|ja|院政}} period, the role of Rōkoku Hakase became symbolic, primarily awarded to members of the {{ill|Kamo clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} or {{ill|Abe clan|ja|阿倍氏}} or their recommended disciples. Figures such as {{ill|Sugano no Suketaka|ja|菅野季親}} and {{ill|Sugano no Suketaka|ja|菅野季長}} became Rōkoku Hakase not for expertise in water clocks but for their skill in annual divination ({{ill|Nensei|ja|年筮}}). Although water clocks were also installed in {{ill|Dazaifu|ja|大宰府}} and {{ill|Mutsu Province|ja|陸奥国}} (and later in {{ill|Dewa Province|ja|出羽国}}), they were managed solely by Morishin-chō without a corresponding Hakase.
== History == Later, [[Emperor Tenmu]] was such a master of astrology and fugue that he took his own divination tools and told fortunes during the [[Jinshin War]]. He also had a deep knowledge of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy, which led to the establishment of the Bureau of Onmyō and Japan's first [[observatory]] in 676, and the use of the term "onmyōji" in 685, which further increased the popularity of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy. In 718, the [[Yōrō Code]] established the Bureau of Onmyō as an internal department of the Ministry of Center, and when it was stipulated that the positions of {{ill|Temmon Hakase|lt=Doctor of Astrology|ja|天文博士}}, {{ill|Onmyō Hakase|lt=Doctor of Onmyō|ja|陰陽博士}}, onmyōji, {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}}, and {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} should be permanently assigned as technical officers, the Bureau of Onmyō became officially in charge of divination along with the [[turtle shell]] diviners who belonged to the [[Department of Divinities]].
== Related Articles == * {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制}} * {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}} * {{ill|Water clock|ja|漏刻}}

{{draft}} {{AFC comment|1=Note: This draft started from a complete copy of [[Onmyōji]] as it has a lot of redlinks with claims I want to keep. I will trim down into just the claim on an individual thing later[[User:Immanuelle|'''Immanuel'''le]] ❤️💚💙 [[User_talk:Immanuelle|(talk to the cutest Wikipedian)]] 01:41, 25 April 2023 (UTC)}} {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} (Rōkoku Hakase, 漏刻博士) is position in the [[Ministry of the Center]] the chief timekeeper.<ref name="titsingh427">Titsingh, Isaac. (1834). {{Google books|18oNAAAAIAAJ|''Annales des empereurs du japon,'' p. 427.|page=427}}</ref><ref>https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/10.7916/d8-3zya-0s65/download</ref><ref>https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/10.7916/D8HD82PN/download</ref><ref>https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/id=8943</ref><ref>https://bazhum.muzhp.pl/media/files/Analecta_Nipponica/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1-s139-202/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1-s139-202.pdf</ref>
The position was a {{ill|Hakase|ja|博士 (文官)}} under the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制}} within the {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}}. The {{ill|Japanese reading|ja|和訓}} (和訓) for this position was "Tokitsukasa" (ときつかさ), while its {{ill|Chinese name|ja|唐名}} was "Shijin" (司辰) or "Keiko-shi" (契壷司). Two individuals typically filled this role, though additional deputy officials ({{ill|Gonkan|ja|権官}}) were occasionally appointed. Officially classified as {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Lower Grade|ja|従七位下}}, individuals of higher ranks, such as the fifth or sixth ranks, were sometimes appointed to this position (as noted in the {{ill|Shokugenshō|ja|職源鈔}}). [[ja:漏刻博士]] The Rōkoku Hakase supervised the {{ill|Morishin-chō|ja|守辰丁}}, a group of 20 individuals selected from {{ill|Shichō|ja|仕丁}}, who guarded the {{ill|Water clocks|ja|漏刻}} and operated them to measure time. At designated times, they would order the Morishin-chō to strike the {{ill|bells|ja|鐘}} located within the Onmyōryō. During the [[Emperor of Japan|Emperor]]'s {{ill|Imperial visits|ja|行幸}}, one Rōkoku Hakase and twelve Morishin-chō were required to accompany the water clock.
In {{ill|Tang dynasty|ja|唐}}, a similar role for a Rōkoku Hakase existed, but the responsibilities were distinct. In Tang China, the practical tasks of water clocks were managed by officials such as Kekkosei (挈壺正), Shijin (司辰), and Rokoku Tenshi (漏刻典事), while the Rōkoku Hakase focused on teaching students of water clocks (Rokokusei). Conversely, in Japan, the practical roles of Kekkosei and related officials were incorporated into the duties of the Rōkoku Hakase. Japan did not establish a Rokokusei system, meaning that Rōkoku Hakase did not have educational duties. This contrasts with the roles of {{ill|Tenmon Hakase|ja|天文博士}} (Astronomy Doctor) and {{ill|Reki Hakase|ja|暦博士}} (Calendar Doctor), who both managed practical tasks and taught students.<ref>Masashi Kinoshita, ''Kodai no Rōkoku to Jikoku Seido'' (Ancient Water Clocks and Time Systems), Yoshikawa Kōbunkan, 2020, ISBN 978-4-642-04657-2, pp. 307–312.</ref>
The water clock system appears to have declined relatively early. By the {{ill|Insei|ja|院政}} period, the role of Rōkoku Hakase became symbolic, primarily awarded to members of the {{ill|Kamo clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} or {{ill|Abe clan|ja|阿倍氏}} or their recommended disciples. Figures such as {{ill|Sugano no Suketaka|ja|菅野季親}} and {{ill|Sugano no Suketaka|ja|菅野季長}} became Rōkoku Hakase not for expertise in water clocks but for their skill in annual divination ({{ill|Nensei|ja|年筮}}). Although water clocks were also installed in {{ill|Dazaifu|ja|大宰府}} and {{ill|Mutsu Province|ja|陸奥国}} (and later in {{ill|Dewa Province|ja|出羽国}}), they were managed solely by Morishin-chō without a corresponding Hakase.
== History == Later, [[Emperor Tenmu]] was such a master of astrology and fugue that he took his own divination tools and told fortunes during the [[Jinshin War]]. He also had a deep knowledge of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy, which led to the establishment of the Bureau of Onmyō and Japan's first [[observatory]] in 676, and the use of the term "onmyōji" in 685, which further increased the popularity of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy. In 718, the [[Yōrō Code]] established the Bureau of Onmyō as an internal department of the Ministry of Center, and when it was stipulated that the positions of {{ill|Temmon Hakase|lt=Doctor of Astrology|ja|天文博士}}, {{ill|Onmyō Hakase|lt=Doctor of Onmyō|ja|陰陽博士}}, onmyōji, {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}}, and {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} should be permanently assigned as technical officers, the Bureau of Onmyō became officially in charge of divination along with the [[turtle shell]] diviners who belonged to the [[Department of Divinities]].
== Related Articles == * {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制}} * {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}} * {{ill|Water clock|ja|漏刻}}

In 718, the [[Yōrō Code]] established the Bureau of Onmyō as an internal department of the Ministry of Center, and when it was stipulated that the positions of {{ill|Temmon Hakase|lt=Doctor of Astrology|ja|天文博士}}, {{ill|Onmyō Hakase|lt=Doctor of Onmyō|ja|陰陽博士}}, onmyōji, {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}}, and {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} should be permanently assigned as technical officers, the Bureau of Onmyō became officially in charge of divination along with the [[turtle shell]] diviners who belonged to the [[Department of Divinities]].

{{draft}} {{AFC comment|1=Note: This draft started from a complete copy of [[Onmyōji]] as it has a lot of redlinks with claims I want to keep. I will trim down into just the claim on an individual thing later[[User:Immanuelle|'''Immanuel'''le]] ❤️💚💙 [[User_talk:Immanuelle|(talk to the cutest Wikipedian)]] 01:41, 25 April 2023 (UTC)}} {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} (Rōkoku Hakase, 漏刻博士) is position in the [[Ministry of the Center]] the chief timekeeper.<ref name="titsingh427">Titsingh, Isaac. (1834). {{Google books|18oNAAAAIAAJ|''Annales des empereurs du japon,'' p. 427.|page=427}}</ref><ref>https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/10.7916/d8-3zya-0s65/download</ref><ref>https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/10.7916/D8HD82PN/download</ref><ref>https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/id=8943</ref><ref>https://bazhum.muzhp.pl/media/files/Analecta_Nipponica/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1-s139-202/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1-s139-202.pdf</ref>
The position was a {{ill|Hakase|ja|博士 (文官)}} under the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制}} within the {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}}. The {{ill|Japanese reading|ja|和訓}} (和訓) for this position was "Tokitsukasa" (ときつかさ), while its {{ill|Chinese name|ja|唐名}} was "Shijin" (司辰) or "Keiko-shi" (契壷司). Two individuals typically filled this role, though additional deputy officials ({{ill|Gonkan|ja|権官}}) were occasionally appointed. Officially classified as {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Lower Grade|ja|従七位下}}, individuals of higher ranks, such as the fifth or sixth ranks, were sometimes appointed to this position (as noted in the {{ill|Shokugenshō|ja|職源鈔}}). [[ja:漏刻博士]] The Rōkoku Hakase supervised the {{ill|Morishin-chō|ja|守辰丁}}, a group of 20 individuals selected from {{ill|Shichō|ja|仕丁}}, who guarded the {{ill|Water clocks|ja|漏刻}} and operated them to measure time. At designated times, they would order the Morishin-chō to strike the {{ill|bells|ja|鐘}} located within the Onmyōryō. During the [[Emperor of Japan|Emperor]]'s {{ill|Imperial visits|ja|行幸}}, one Rōkoku Hakase and twelve Morishin-chō were required to accompany the water clock.
In {{ill|Tang dynasty|ja|唐}}, a similar role for a Rōkoku Hakase existed, but the responsibilities were distinct. In Tang China, the practical tasks of water clocks were managed by officials such as Kekkosei (挈壺正), Shijin (司辰), and Rokoku Tenshi (漏刻典事), while the Rōkoku Hakase focused on teaching students of water clocks (Rokokusei). Conversely, in Japan, the practical roles of Kekkosei and related officials were incorporated into the duties of the Rōkoku Hakase. Japan did not establish a Rokokusei system, meaning that Rōkoku Hakase did not have educational duties. This contrasts with the roles of {{ill|Tenmon Hakase|ja|天文博士}} (Astronomy Doctor) and {{ill|Reki Hakase|ja|暦博士}} (Calendar Doctor), who both managed practical tasks and taught students.<ref>Masashi Kinoshita, ''Kodai no Rōkoku to Jikoku Seido'' (Ancient Water Clocks and Time Systems), Yoshikawa Kōbunkan, 2020, ISBN 978-4-642-04657-2, pp. 307–312.</ref>
The water clock system appears to have declined relatively early. By the {{ill|Insei|ja|院政}} period, the role of Rōkoku Hakase became symbolic, primarily awarded to members of the {{ill|Kamo clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} or {{ill|Abe clan|ja|阿倍氏}} or their recommended disciples. Figures such as {{ill|Sugano no Suketaka|ja|菅野季親}} and {{ill|Sugano no Suketaka|ja|菅野季長}} became Rōkoku Hakase not for expertise in water clocks but for their skill in annual divination ({{ill|Nensei|ja|年筮}}). Although water clocks were also installed in {{ill|Dazaifu|ja|大宰府}} and {{ill|Mutsu Province|ja|陸奥国}} (and later in {{ill|Dewa Province|ja|出羽国}}), they were managed solely by Morishin-chō without a corresponding Hakase.
== History == Later, [[Emperor Tenmu]] was such a master of astrology and fugue that he took his own divination tools and told fortunes during the [[Jinshin War]]. He also had a deep knowledge of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy, which led to the establishment of the Bureau of Onmyō and Japan's first [[observatory]] in 676, and the use of the term "onmyōji" in 685, which further increased the popularity of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy. In 718, the [[Yōrō Code]] established the Bureau of Onmyō as an internal department of the Ministry of Center, and when it was stipulated that the positions of {{ill|Temmon Hakase|lt=Doctor of Astrology|ja|天文博士}}, {{ill|Onmyō Hakase|lt=Doctor of Onmyō|ja|陰陽博士}}, onmyōji, {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}}, and {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} should be permanently assigned as technical officers, the Bureau of Onmyō became officially in charge of divination along with the [[turtle shell]] diviners who belonged to the [[Department of Divinities]].

I will trim down into just the claim on an individual thing later[[User:Immanuelle|'''Immanuel'''le]] ❤️💚💙 [[User_talk:Immanuelle|(talk to the cutest Wikipedian)]] 01:41, 25 April 2023 (UTC)}} {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} (Rōkoku Hakase, 漏刻博士) is position in the [[Ministry of the Center]] the chief timekeeper.<ref name="titsingh427">Titsingh, Isaac. (1834). {{Google books|18oNAAAAIAAJ|''Annales des empereurs du japon,'' p. 427.|page=427}}</ref><ref>https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/10.7916/d8-3zya-0s65/download</ref><ref>https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/10.7916/D8HD82PN/download</ref><ref>https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/id=8943</ref><ref>https://bazhum.muzhp.pl/media/files/Analecta_Nipponica/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1-s139-202/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1-s139-202.pdf</ref>
The position was a {{ill|Hakase|ja|博士 (文官)}} under the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制}} within the {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}}. The {{ill|Japanese reading|ja|和訓}} (和訓) for this position was "Tokitsukasa" (ときつかさ), while its {{ill|Chinese name|ja|唐名}} was "Shijin" (司辰) or "Keiko-shi" (契壷司). Two individuals typically filled this role, though additional deputy officials ({{ill|Gonkan|ja|権官}}) were occasionally appointed. Officially classified as {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Lower Grade|ja|従七位下}}, individuals of higher ranks, such as the fifth or sixth ranks, were sometimes appointed to this position (as noted in the {{ill|Shokugenshō|ja|職源鈔}}). [[ja:漏刻博士]] The Rōkoku Hakase supervised the {{ill|Morishin-chō|ja|守辰丁}}, a group of 20 individuals selected from {{ill|Shichō|ja|仕丁}}, who guarded the {{ill|Water clocks|ja|漏刻}} and operated them to measure time. At designated times, they would order the Morishin-chō to strike the {{ill|bells|ja|鐘}} located within the Onmyōryō. During the [[Emperor of Japan|Emperor]]'s {{ill|Imperial visits|ja|行幸}}, one Rōkoku Hakase and twelve Morishin-chō were required to accompany the water clock.
In {{ill|Tang dynasty|ja|唐}}, a similar role for a Rōkoku Hakase existed, but the responsibilities were distinct. In Tang China, the practical tasks of water clocks were managed by officials such as Kekkosei (挈壺正), Shijin (司辰), and Rokoku Tenshi (漏刻典事), while the Rōkoku Hakase focused on teaching students of water clocks (Rokokusei). Conversely, in Japan, the practical roles of Kekkosei and related officials were incorporated into the duties of the Rōkoku Hakase. Japan did not establish a Rokokusei system, meaning that Rōkoku Hakase did not have educational duties. This contrasts with the roles of {{ill|Tenmon Hakase|ja|天文博士}} (Astronomy Doctor) and {{ill|Reki Hakase|ja|暦博士}} (Calendar Doctor), who both managed practical tasks and taught students.<ref>Masashi Kinoshita, ''Kodai no Rōkoku to Jikoku Seido'' (Ancient Water Clocks and Time Systems), Yoshikawa Kōbunkan, 2020, ISBN 978-4-642-04657-2, pp. 307–312.</ref>
The water clock system appears to have declined relatively early. By the {{ill|Insei|ja|院政}} period, the role of Rōkoku Hakase became symbolic, primarily awarded to members of the {{ill|Kamo clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} or {{ill|Abe clan|ja|阿倍氏}} or their recommended disciples. Figures such as {{ill|Sugano no Suketaka|ja|菅野季親}} and {{ill|Sugano no Suketaka|ja|菅野季長}} became Rōkoku Hakase not for expertise in water clocks but for their skill in annual divination ({{ill|Nensei|ja|年筮}}). Although water clocks were also installed in {{ill|Dazaifu|ja|大宰府}} and {{ill|Mutsu Province|ja|陸奥国}} (and later in {{ill|Dewa Province|ja|出羽国}}), they were managed solely by Morishin-chō without a corresponding Hakase.
== History == Later, [[Emperor Tenmu]] was such a master of astrology and fugue that he took his own divination tools and told fortunes during the [[Jinshin War]]. He also had a deep knowledge of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy, which led to the establishment of the Bureau of Onmyō and Japan's first [[observatory]] in 676, and the use of the term "onmyōji" in 685, which further increased the popularity of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy. In 718, the [[Yōrō Code]] established the Bureau of Onmyō as an internal department of the Ministry of Center, and when it was stipulated that the positions of {{ill|Temmon Hakase|lt=Doctor of Astrology|ja|天文博士}}, {{ill|Onmyō Hakase|lt=Doctor of Onmyō|ja|陰陽博士}}, onmyōji, {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}}, and {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} should be permanently assigned as technical officers, the Bureau of Onmyō became officially in charge of divination along with the [[turtle shell]] diviners who belonged to the [[Department of Divinities]].

revision.text:
{{draft}} {{AFC comment|1=Note: This draft started from a complete copy of [[Onmyōji]] as it has a lot of redlinks with claims I want to keep. I will trim down into just the claim on an individual thing later[[User:Immanuelle|'''Immanuel'''le]] ❤️💚💙 [[User_talk:Immanuelle|(talk to the cutest Wikipedian)]] 01:41, 25 April 2023 (UTC)}} {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} (Rōkoku Hakase, 漏刻博士) is position in the [[Ministry of the Center]] the chief timekeeper.<ref name="titsingh427">Titsingh, Isaac. (1834). {{Google books|18oNAAAAIAAJ|''Annales des empereurs du japon,'' p. 427.|page=427}}</ref><ref>https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/10.7916/d8-3zya-0s65/download</ref><ref>https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/10.7916/D8HD82PN/download</ref><ref>https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/id=8943</ref><ref>https://bazhum.muzhp.pl/media/files/Analecta_Nipponica/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1-s139-202/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1-s139-202.pdf</ref>
The position was a {{ill|Hakase|ja|博士 (文官)}} under the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制}} within the {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}}. The {{ill|Japanese reading|ja|和訓}} (和訓) for this position was "Tokitsukasa" (ときつかさ), while its {{ill|Chinese name|ja|唐名}} was "Shijin" (司辰) or "Keiko-shi" (契壷司). Two individuals typically filled this role, though additional deputy officials ({{ill|Gonkan|ja|権官}}) were occasionally appointed. Officially classified as {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Lower Grade|ja|従七位下}}, individuals of higher ranks, such as the fifth or sixth ranks, were sometimes appointed to this position (as noted in the {{ill|Shokugenshō|ja|職源鈔}}). [[ja:漏刻博士]] The Rōkoku Hakase supervised the {{ill|Morishin-chō|ja|守辰丁}}, a group of 20 individuals selected from {{ill|Shichō|ja|仕丁}}, who guarded the {{ill|Water clocks|ja|漏刻}} and operated them to measure time. At designated times, they would order the Morishin-chō to strike the {{ill|bells|ja|鐘}} located within the Onmyōryō. During the [[Emperor of Japan|Emperor]]'s {{ill|Imperial visits|ja|行幸}}, one Rōkoku Hakase and twelve Morishin-chō were required to accompany the water clock.
In {{ill|Tang dynasty|ja|唐}}, a similar role for a Rōkoku Hakase existed, but the responsibilities were distinct. In Tang China, the practical tasks of water clocks were managed by officials such as Kekkosei (挈壺正), Shijin (司辰), and Rokoku Tenshi (漏刻典事), while the Rōkoku Hakase focused on teaching students of water clocks (Rokokusei). Conversely, in Japan, the practical roles of Kekkosei and related officials were incorporated into the duties of the Rōkoku Hakase. Japan did not establish a Rokokusei system, meaning that Rōkoku Hakase did not have educational duties. This contrasts with the roles of {{ill|Tenmon Hakase|ja|天文博士}} (Astronomy Doctor) and {{ill|Reki Hakase|ja|暦博士}} (Calendar Doctor), who both managed practical tasks and taught students.<ref>Masashi Kinoshita, ''Kodai no Rōkoku to Jikoku Seido'' (Ancient Water Clocks and Time Systems), Yoshikawa Kōbunkan, 2020, ISBN 978-4-642-04657-2, pp. 307–312.</ref>
The water clock system appears to have declined relatively early. By the {{ill|Insei|ja|院政}} period, the role of Rōkoku Hakase became symbolic, primarily awarded to members of the {{ill|Kamo clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} or {{ill|Abe clan|ja|阿倍氏}} or their recommended disciples. Figures such as {{ill|Sugano no Suketaka|ja|菅野季親}} and {{ill|Sugano no Suketaka|ja|菅野季長}} became Rōkoku Hakase not for expertise in water clocks but for their skill in annual divination ({{ill|Nensei|ja|年筮}}). Although water clocks were also installed in {{ill|Dazaifu|ja|大宰府}} and {{ill|Mutsu Province|ja|陸奥国}} (and later in {{ill|Dewa Province|ja|出羽国}}), they were managed solely by Morishin-chō without a corresponding Hakase.
== History == Later, [[Emperor Tenmu]] was such a master of astrology and fugue that he took his own divination tools and told fortunes during the [[Jinshin War]]. He also had a deep knowledge of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy, which led to the establishment of the Bureau of Onmyō and Japan's first [[observatory]] in 676, and the use of the term "onmyōji" in 685, which further increased the popularity of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy. In 718, the [[Yōrō Code]] established the Bureau of Onmyō as an internal department of the Ministry of Center, and when it was stipulated that the positions of {{ill|Temmon Hakase|lt=Doctor of Astrology|ja|天文博士}}, {{ill|Onmyō Hakase|lt=Doctor of Onmyō|ja|陰陽博士}}, onmyōji, {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}}, and {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} should be permanently assigned as technical officers, the Bureau of Onmyō became officially in charge of divination along with the [[turtle shell]] diviners who belonged to the [[Department of Divinities]].
== Related Articles == * {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制}} * {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}} * {{ill|Water clock|ja|漏刻}}

He also had a deep knowledge of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy, which led to the establishment of the Bureau of Onmyō and Japan's first [[observatory]] in 676, and the use of the term "onmyōji" in 685, which further increased the popularity of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy. In 718, the [[Yōrō Code]] established the Bureau of Onmyō as an internal department of the Ministry of Center, and when it was stipulated that the positions of {{ill|Temmon Hakase|lt=Doctor of Astrology|ja|天文博士}}, {{ill|Onmyō Hakase|lt=Doctor of Onmyō|ja|陰陽博士}}, onmyōji, {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}}, and {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} should be permanently assigned as technical officers, the Bureau of Onmyō became officially in charge of divination along with the [[turtle shell]] diviners who belonged to the [[Department of Divinities]].

{{draft}} {{AFC comment|1=Note: This draft started from a complete copy of [[Onmyōji]] as it has a lot of redlinks with claims I want to keep. I will trim down into just the claim on an individual thing later[[User:Immanuelle|'''Immanuel'''le]] ❤️💚💙 [[User_talk:Immanuelle|(talk to the cutest Wikipedian)]] 01:41, 25 April 2023 (UTC)}} {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} (Rōkoku Hakase, 漏刻博士) is position in the [[Ministry of the Center]] the chief timekeeper.<ref name="titsingh427">Titsingh, Isaac. (1834). {{Google books|18oNAAAAIAAJ|''Annales des empereurs du japon,'' p. 427.|page=427}}</ref><ref>https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/10.7916/d8-3zya-0s65/download</ref><ref>https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/10.7916/D8HD82PN/download</ref><ref>https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/id=8943</ref><ref>https://bazhum.muzhp.pl/media/files/Analecta_Nipponica/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1-s139-202/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1-s139-202.pdf</ref>
The position was a {{ill|Hakase|ja|博士 (文官)}} under the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制}} within the {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}}. The {{ill|Japanese reading|ja|和訓}} (和訓) for this position was "Tokitsukasa" (ときつかさ), while its {{ill|Chinese name|ja|唐名}} was "Shijin" (司辰) or "Keiko-shi" (契壷司). Two individuals typically filled this role, though additional deputy officials ({{ill|Gonkan|ja|権官}}) were occasionally appointed. Officially classified as {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Lower Grade|ja|従七位下}}, individuals of higher ranks, such as the fifth or sixth ranks, were sometimes appointed to this position (as noted in the {{ill|Shokugenshō|ja|職源鈔}}). [[ja:漏刻博士]] The Rōkoku Hakase supervised the {{ill|Morishin-chō|ja|守辰丁}}, a group of 20 individuals selected from {{ill|Shichō|ja|仕丁}}, who guarded the {{ill|Water clocks|ja|漏刻}} and operated them to measure time. At designated times, they would order the Morishin-chō to strike the {{ill|bells|ja|鐘}} located within the Onmyōryō. During the [[Emperor of Japan|Emperor]]'s {{ill|Imperial visits|ja|行幸}}, one Rōkoku Hakase and twelve Morishin-chō were required to accompany the water clock.
In {{ill|Tang dynasty|ja|唐}}, a similar role for a Rōkoku Hakase existed, but the responsibilities were distinct. In Tang China, the practical tasks of water clocks were managed by officials such as Kekkosei (挈壺正), Shijin (司辰), and Rokoku Tenshi (漏刻典事), while the Rōkoku Hakase focused on teaching students of water clocks (Rokokusei). Conversely, in Japan, the practical roles of Kekkosei and related officials were incorporated into the duties of the Rōkoku Hakase. Japan did not establish a Rokokusei system, meaning that Rōkoku Hakase did not have educational duties. This contrasts with the roles of {{ill|Tenmon Hakase|ja|天文博士}} (Astronomy Doctor) and {{ill|Reki Hakase|ja|暦博士}} (Calendar Doctor), who both managed practical tasks and taught students.<ref>Masashi Kinoshita, ''Kodai no Rōkoku to Jikoku Seido'' (Ancient Water Clocks and Time Systems), Yoshikawa Kōbunkan, 2020, ISBN 978-4-642-04657-2, pp. 307–312.</ref>
The water clock system appears to have declined relatively early. By the {{ill|Insei|ja|院政}} period, the role of Rōkoku Hakase became symbolic, primarily awarded to members of the {{ill|Kamo clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} or {{ill|Abe clan|ja|阿倍氏}} or their recommended disciples. Figures such as {{ill|Sugano no Suketaka|ja|菅野季親}} and {{ill|Sugano no Suketaka|ja|菅野季長}} became Rōkoku Hakase not for expertise in water clocks but for their skill in annual divination ({{ill|Nensei|ja|年筮}}). Although water clocks were also installed in {{ill|Dazaifu|ja|大宰府}} and {{ill|Mutsu Province|ja|陸奥国}} (and later in {{ill|Dewa Province|ja|出羽国}}), they were managed solely by Morishin-chō without a corresponding Hakase.
== History == Later, [[Emperor Tenmu]] was such a master of astrology and fugue that he took his own divination tools and told fortunes during the [[Jinshin War]]. He also had a deep knowledge of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy, which led to the establishment of the Bureau of Onmyō and Japan's first [[observatory]] in 676, and the use of the term "onmyōji" in 685, which further increased the popularity of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy. In 718, the [[Yōrō Code]] established the Bureau of Onmyō as an internal department of the Ministry of Center, and when it was stipulated that the positions of {{ill|Temmon Hakase|lt=Doctor of Astrology|ja|天文博士}}, {{ill|Onmyō Hakase|lt=Doctor of Onmyō|ja|陰陽博士}}, onmyōji, {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}}, and {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} should be permanently assigned as technical officers, the Bureau of Onmyō became officially in charge of divination along with the [[turtle shell]] diviners who belonged to the [[Department of Divinities]].

{{draft}} {{AFC comment|1=Note: This draft started from a complete copy of [[Onmyōji]] as it has a lot of redlinks with claims I want to keep. I will trim down into just the claim on an individual thing later[[User:Immanuelle|'''Immanuel'''le]] ❤️💚💙 [[User_talk:Immanuelle|(talk to the cutest Wikipedian)]] 01:41, 25 April 2023 (UTC)}} {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} (Rōkoku Hakase, 漏刻博士) is position in the [[Ministry of the Center]] the chief timekeeper.<ref name="titsingh427">Titsingh, Isaac. (1834). {{Google books|18oNAAAAIAAJ|''Annales des empereurs du japon,'' p. 427.|page=427}}</ref><ref>https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/10.7916/d8-3zya-0s65/download</ref><ref>https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/10.7916/D8HD82PN/download</ref><ref>https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/id=8943</ref><ref>https://bazhum.muzhp.pl/media/files/Analecta_Nipponica/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1-s139-202/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1-s139-202.pdf</ref>
The position was a {{ill|Hakase|ja|博士 (文官)}} under the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制}} within the {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}}. The {{ill|Japanese reading|ja|和訓}} (和訓) for this position was "Tokitsukasa" (ときつかさ), while its {{ill|Chinese name|ja|唐名}} was "Shijin" (司辰) or "Keiko-shi" (契壷司). Two individuals typically filled this role, though additional deputy officials ({{ill|Gonkan|ja|権官}}) were occasionally appointed. Officially classified as {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Lower Grade|ja|従七位下}}, individuals of higher ranks, such as the fifth or sixth ranks, were sometimes appointed to this position (as noted in the {{ill|Shokugenshō|ja|職源鈔}}). [[ja:漏刻博士]] The Rōkoku Hakase supervised the {{ill|Morishin-chō|ja|守辰丁}}, a group of 20 individuals selected from {{ill|Shichō|ja|仕丁}}, who guarded the {{ill|Water clocks|ja|漏刻}} and operated them to measure time. At designated times, they would order the Morishin-chō to strike the {{ill|bells|ja|鐘}} located within the Onmyōryō. During the [[Emperor of Japan|Emperor]]'s {{ill|Imperial visits|ja|行幸}}, one Rōkoku Hakase and twelve Morishin-chō were required to accompany the water clock.
In {{ill|Tang dynasty|ja|唐}}, a similar role for a Rōkoku Hakase existed, but the responsibilities were distinct. In Tang China, the practical tasks of water clocks were managed by officials such as Kekkosei (挈壺正), Shijin (司辰), and Rokoku Tenshi (漏刻典事), while the Rōkoku Hakase focused on teaching students of water clocks (Rokokusei). Conversely, in Japan, the practical roles of Kekkosei and related officials were incorporated into the duties of the Rōkoku Hakase. Japan did not establish a Rokokusei system, meaning that Rōkoku Hakase did not have educational duties. This contrasts with the roles of {{ill|Tenmon Hakase|ja|天文博士}} (Astronomy Doctor) and {{ill|Reki Hakase|ja|暦博士}} (Calendar Doctor), who both managed practical tasks and taught students.<ref>Masashi Kinoshita, ''Kodai no Rōkoku to Jikoku Seido'' (Ancient Water Clocks and Time Systems), Yoshikawa Kōbunkan, 2020, ISBN 978-4-642-04657-2, pp. 307–312.</ref>
The water clock system appears to have declined relatively early. By the {{ill|Insei|ja|院政}} period, the role of Rōkoku Hakase became symbolic, primarily awarded to members of the {{ill|Kamo clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} or {{ill|Abe clan|ja|阿倍氏}} or their recommended disciples. Figures such as {{ill|Sugano no Suketaka|ja|菅野季親}} and {{ill|Sugano no Suketaka|ja|菅野季長}} became Rōkoku Hakase not for expertise in water clocks but for their skill in annual divination ({{ill|Nensei|ja|年筮}}). Although water clocks were also installed in {{ill|Dazaifu|ja|大宰府}} and {{ill|Mutsu Province|ja|陸奥国}} (and later in {{ill|Dewa Province|ja|出羽国}}), they were managed solely by Morishin-chō without a corresponding Hakase.
== History == Later, [[Emperor Tenmu]] was such a master of astrology and fugue that he took his own divination tools and told fortunes during the [[Jinshin War]]. He also had a deep knowledge of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy, which led to the establishment of the Bureau of Onmyō and Japan's first [[observatory]] in 676, and the use of the term "onmyōji" in 685, which further increased the popularity of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy. In 718, the [[Yōrō Code]] established the Bureau of Onmyō as an internal department of the Ministry of Center, and when it was stipulated that the positions of {{ill|Temmon Hakase|lt=Doctor of Astrology|ja|天文博士}}, {{ill|Onmyō Hakase|lt=Doctor of Onmyō|ja|陰陽博士}}, onmyōji, {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}}, and {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} should be permanently assigned as technical officers, the Bureau of Onmyō became officially in charge of divination along with the [[turtle shell]] diviners who belonged to the [[Department of Divinities]].

{{draft}} {{AFC comment|1=Note: This draft started from a complete copy of [[Onmyōji]] as it has a lot of redlinks with claims I want to keep. I will trim down into just the claim on an individual thing later[[User:Immanuelle|'''Immanuel'''le]] ❤️💚💙 [[User_talk:Immanuelle|(talk to the cutest Wikipedian)]] 01:41, 25 April 2023 (UTC)}} {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} (Rōkoku Hakase, 漏刻博士) is position in the [[Ministry of the Center]] the chief timekeeper.<ref name="titsingh427">Titsingh, Isaac. (1834). {{Google books|18oNAAAAIAAJ|''Annales des empereurs du japon,'' p. 427.|page=427}}</ref><ref>https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/10.7916/d8-3zya-0s65/download</ref><ref>https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/10.7916/D8HD82PN/download</ref><ref>https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/id=8943</ref><ref>https://bazhum.muzhp.pl/media/files/Analecta_Nipponica/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1-s139-202/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1-s139-202.pdf</ref>
The position was a {{ill|Hakase|ja|博士 (文官)}} under the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制}} within the {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}}. The {{ill|Japanese reading|ja|和訓}} (和訓) for this position was "Tokitsukasa" (ときつかさ), while its {{ill|Chinese name|ja|唐名}} was "Shijin" (司辰) or "Keiko-shi" (契壷司). Two individuals typically filled this role, though additional deputy officials ({{ill|Gonkan|ja|権官}}) were occasionally appointed. Officially classified as {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Lower Grade|ja|従七位下}}, individuals of higher ranks, such as the fifth or sixth ranks, were sometimes appointed to this position (as noted in the {{ill|Shokugenshō|ja|職源鈔}}). [[ja:漏刻博士]] The Rōkoku Hakase supervised the {{ill|Morishin-chō|ja|守辰丁}}, a group of 20 individuals selected from {{ill|Shichō|ja|仕丁}}, who guarded the {{ill|Water clocks|ja|漏刻}} and operated them to measure time. At designated times, they would order the Morishin-chō to strike the {{ill|bells|ja|鐘}} located within the Onmyōryō. During the [[Emperor of Japan|Emperor]]'s {{ill|Imperial visits|ja|行幸}}, one Rōkoku Hakase and twelve Morishin-chō were required to accompany the water clock.
In {{ill|Tang dynasty|ja|唐}}, a similar role for a Rōkoku Hakase existed, but the responsibilities were distinct. In Tang China, the practical tasks of water clocks were managed by officials such as Kekkosei (挈壺正), Shijin (司辰), and Rokoku Tenshi (漏刻典事), while the Rōkoku Hakase focused on teaching students of water clocks (Rokokusei). Conversely, in Japan, the practical roles of Kekkosei and related officials were incorporated into the duties of the Rōkoku Hakase. Japan did not establish a Rokokusei system, meaning that Rōkoku Hakase did not have educational duties. This contrasts with the roles of {{ill|Tenmon Hakase|ja|天文博士}} (Astronomy Doctor) and {{ill|Reki Hakase|ja|暦博士}} (Calendar Doctor), who both managed practical tasks and taught students.<ref>Masashi Kinoshita, ''Kodai no Rōkoku to Jikoku Seido'' (Ancient Water Clocks and Time Systems), Yoshikawa Kōbunkan, 2020, ISBN 978-4-642-04657-2, pp. 307–312.</ref>
The water clock system appears to have declined relatively early. By the {{ill|Insei|ja|院政}} period, the role of Rōkoku Hakase became symbolic, primarily awarded to members of the {{ill|Kamo clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} or {{ill|Abe clan|ja|阿倍氏}} or their recommended disciples. Figures such as {{ill|Sugano no Suketaka|ja|菅野季親}} and {{ill|Sugano no Suketaka|ja|菅野季長}} became Rōkoku Hakase not for expertise in water clocks but for their skill in annual divination ({{ill|Nensei|ja|年筮}}). Although water clocks were also installed in {{ill|Dazaifu|ja|大宰府}} and {{ill|Mutsu Province|ja|陸奥国}} (and later in {{ill|Dewa Province|ja|出羽国}}), they were managed solely by Morishin-chō without a corresponding Hakase.
== History == Later, [[Emperor Tenmu]] was such a master of astrology and fugue that he took his own divination tools and told fortunes during the [[Jinshin War]]. He also had a deep knowledge of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy, which led to the establishment of the Bureau of Onmyō and Japan's first [[observatory]] in 676, and the use of the term "onmyōji" in 685, which further increased the popularity of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy. In 718, the [[Yōrō Code]] established the Bureau of Onmyō as an internal department of the Ministry of Center, and when it was stipulated that the positions of {{ill|Temmon Hakase|lt=Doctor of Astrology|ja|天文博士}}, {{ill|Onmyō Hakase|lt=Doctor of Onmyō|ja|陰陽博士}}, onmyōji, {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}}, and {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} should be permanently assigned as technical officers, the Bureau of Onmyō became officially in charge of divination along with the [[turtle shell]] diviners who belonged to the [[Department of Divinities]].
