(1834). {{Google books|18oNAAAAIAAJ|''Annales des empereurs du japon,'' p. 427.|page=427}}</ref><ref>https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/10.7916/d8-3zya-0s65/download</ref><ref>https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/10.7916/D8HD82PN/download</ref><ref>https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/id=8943</ref><ref>https://bazhum.muzhp.pl/media/files/Analecta_Nipponica/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1-s139-202/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1-s139-202.pdf</ref>
The position was a {{ill|Hakase|ja|博士 (文官)}} under the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制}} within the {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}}. The {{ill|Japanese reading|ja|和訓}} (和訓) for this position was "Tokitsukasa" (ときつかさ), while its {{ill|Chinese name|ja|唐名}} was "Shijin" (司辰) or "Keiko-shi" (契壷司). Two individuals typically filled this role, though additional deputy officials ({{ill|Gonkan|ja|権官}}) were occasionally appointed. Officially classified as {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Lower Grade|ja|従七位下}}, individuals of higher ranks, such as the fifth or sixth ranks, were sometimes appointed to this position (as noted in the {{ill|Shokugenshō|ja|職源鈔}}). [[ja:漏刻博士]] The Rōkoku Hakase supervised the {{ill|Morishin-chō|ja|守辰丁}}, a group of 20 individuals selected from {{ill|Shichō|ja|仕丁}}, who guarded the {{ill|Water clocks|ja|漏刻}} and operated them to measure time. At designated times, they would order the Morishin-chō to strike the {{ill|bells|ja|鐘}} located within the Onmyōryō. During the [[Emperor of Japan|Emperor]]'s {{ill|Imperial visits|ja|行幸}}, one Rōkoku Hakase and twelve Morishin-chō were required to accompany the water clock.
In {{ill|Tang dynasty|ja|唐}}, a similar role for a Rōkoku Hakase existed, but the responsibilities were distinct. In Tang China, the practical tasks of water clocks were managed by officials such as Kekkosei (挈壺正), Shijin (司辰), and Rokoku Tenshi (漏刻典事), while the Rōkoku Hakase focused on teaching students of water clocks (Rokokusei). Conversely, in Japan, the practical roles of Kekkosei and related officials were incorporated into the duties of the Rōkoku Hakase. Japan did not establish a Rokokusei system, meaning that Rōkoku Hakase did not have educational duties. This contrasts with the roles of {{ill|Tenmon Hakase|ja|天文博士}} (Astronomy Doctor) and {{ill|Reki Hakase|ja|暦博士}} (Calendar Doctor), who both managed practical tasks and taught students.<ref>Masashi Kinoshita, ''Kodai no Rōkoku to Jikoku Seido'' (Ancient Water Clocks and Time Systems), Yoshikawa Kōbunkan, 2020, ISBN 978-4-642-04657-2, pp. 307–312.</ref>
The water clock system appears to have declined relatively early. By the {{ill|Insei|ja|院政}} period, the role of Rōkoku Hakase became symbolic, primarily awarded to members of the {{ill|Kamo clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} or {{ill|Abe clan|ja|阿倍氏}} or their recommended disciples. Figures such as {{ill|Sugano no Suketaka|ja|菅野季親}} and {{ill|Sugano no Suketaka|ja|菅野季長}} became Rōkoku Hakase not for expertise in water clocks but for their skill in annual divination ({{ill|Nensei|ja|年筮}}). Although water clocks were also installed in {{ill|Dazaifu|ja|大宰府}} and {{ill|Mutsu Province|ja|陸奥国}} (and later in {{ill|Dewa Province|ja|出羽国}}), they were managed solely by Morishin-chō without a corresponding Hakase.
== History == Later, [[Emperor Tenmu]] was such a master of astrology and fugue that he took his own divination tools and told fortunes during the [[Jinshin War]]. He also had a deep knowledge of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy, which led to the establishment of the Bureau of Onmyō and Japan's first [[observatory]] in 676, and the use of the term "onmyōji" in 685, which further increased the popularity of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy. In 718, the [[Yōrō Code]] established the Bureau of Onmyō as an internal department of the Ministry of Center, and when it was stipulated that the positions of {{ill|Temmon Hakase|lt=Doctor of Astrology|ja|天文博士}}, {{ill|Onmyō Hakase|lt=Doctor of Onmyō|ja|陰陽博士}}, onmyōji, {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}}, and {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} should be permanently assigned as technical officers, the Bureau of Onmyō became officially in charge of divination along with the [[turtle shell]] diviners who belonged to the [[Department of Divinities]].

Go to [[:en:Wikipedia:Requests for undeletion]] to request undeletion of original page [[:en:draft:Rōkoku Hakase]][[en:draft:Rōkoku Hakase]] and import the revisions to here for attribution. View on everybodywiki here [[:every:Rōkoku Hakase|Rōkoku Hakase]]. [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 21:01, 16 February 2025 (UTC)}}{{draft}} {{Promising draft|reason=the high amount of work put into it over a long time, see edit history}} {{afc comment|1=This page was originally created by Immanuelle as a wikipedia draft. It was then automatically transferred to everybodywiki and recovered from there. In the future it will be good to import the revisions. Check page history in case this page was moved, since the everybodywiki page may have been under a different title[[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 20:10, 11 February 2025 (UTC)}} {{draft}} {{AFC comment|1=Note: This draft started from a complete copy of [[Onmyōji]] as it has a lot of redlinks with claims I want to keep. I will trim down into just the claim on an individual thing later[[User:Immanuelle|'''Immanuel'''le]] ❤️💚💙 [[User_talk:Immanuelle|(talk to the cutest Wikipedian)]] 01:41, 25 April 2023 (UTC)}} {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} (Rōkoku Hakase, 漏刻博士) is position in the [[Ministry of the Center]] the chief timekeeper.<ref name="titsingh427">Titsingh, Isaac. (1834). {{Google books|18oNAAAAIAAJ|''Annales des empereurs du japon,'' p. 427.|page=427}}</ref><ref>https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/10.7916/d8-3zya-0s65/download</ref><ref>https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/10.7916/D8HD82PN/download</ref><ref>https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/id=8943</ref><ref>https://bazhum.muzhp.pl/media/files/Analecta_Nipponica/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1-s139-202/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1-s139-202.pdf</ref>
The position was a {{ill|Hakase|ja|博士 (文官)}} under the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制}} within the {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}}. The {{ill|Japanese reading|ja|和訓}} (和訓) for this position was "Tokitsukasa" (ときつかさ), while its {{ill|Chinese name|ja|唐名}} was "Shijin" (司辰) or "Keiko-shi" (契壷司). Two individuals typically filled this role, though additional deputy officials ({{ill|Gonkan|ja|権官}}) were occasionally appointed. Officially classified as {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Lower Grade|ja|従七位下}}, individuals of higher ranks, such as the fifth or sixth ranks, were sometimes appointed to this position (as noted in the {{ill|Shokugenshō|ja|職源鈔}}). [[ja:漏刻博士]] The Rōkoku Hakase supervised the {{ill|Morishin-chō|ja|守辰丁}}, a group of 20 individuals selected from {{ill|Shichō|ja|仕丁}}, who guarded the {{ill|Water clocks|ja|漏刻}} and operated them to measure time. At designated times, they would order the Morishin-chō to strike the {{ill|bells|ja|鐘}} located within the Onmyōryō. During the [[Emperor of Japan|Emperor]]'s {{ill|Imperial visits|ja|行幸}}, one Rōkoku Hakase and twelve Morishin-chō were required to accompany the water clock.
In {{ill|Tang dynasty|ja|唐}}, a similar role for a Rōkoku Hakase existed, but the responsibilities were distinct. In Tang China, the practical tasks of water clocks were managed by officials such as Kekkosei (挈壺正), Shijin (司辰), and Rokoku Tenshi (漏刻典事), while the Rōkoku Hakase focused on teaching students of water clocks (Rokokusei). Conversely, in Japan, the practical roles of Kekkosei and related officials were incorporated into the duties of the Rōkoku Hakase. Japan did not establish a Rokokusei system, meaning that Rōkoku Hakase did not have educational duties. This contrasts with the roles of {{ill|Tenmon Hakase|ja|天文博士}} (Astronomy Doctor) and {{ill|Reki Hakase|ja|暦博士}} (Calendar Doctor), who both managed practical tasks and taught students.<ref>Masashi Kinoshita, ''Kodai no Rōkoku to Jikoku Seido'' (Ancient Water Clocks and Time Systems), Yoshikawa Kōbunkan, 2020, ISBN 978-4-642-04657-2, pp. 307–312.</ref>
The water clock system appears to have declined relatively early. By the {{ill|Insei|ja|院政}} period, the role of Rōkoku Hakase became symbolic, primarily awarded to members of the {{ill|Kamo clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} or {{ill|Abe clan|ja|阿倍氏}} or their recommended disciples. Figures such as {{ill|Sugano no Suketaka|ja|菅野季親}} and {{ill|Sugano no Suketaka|ja|菅野季長}} became Rōkoku Hakase not for expertise in water clocks but for their skill in annual divination ({{ill|Nensei|ja|年筮}}). Although water clocks were also installed in {{ill|Dazaifu|ja|大宰府}} and {{ill|Mutsu Province|ja|陸奥国}} (and later in {{ill|Dewa Province|ja|出羽国}}), they were managed solely by Morishin-chō without a corresponding Hakase.
== History == Later, [[Emperor Tenmu]] was such a master of astrology and fugue that he took his own divination tools and told fortunes during the [[Jinshin War]]. He also had a deep knowledge of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy, which led to the establishment of the Bureau of Onmyō and Japan's first [[observatory]] in 676, and the use of the term "onmyōji" in 685, which further increased the popularity of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy. In 718, the [[Yōrō Code]] established the Bureau of Onmyō as an internal department of the Ministry of Center, and when it was stipulated that the positions of {{ill|Temmon Hakase|lt=Doctor of Astrology|ja|天文博士}}, {{ill|Onmyō Hakase|lt=Doctor of Onmyō|ja|陰陽博士}}, onmyōji, {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}}, and {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} should be permanently assigned as technical officers, the Bureau of Onmyō became officially in charge of divination along with the [[turtle shell]] diviners who belonged to the [[Department of Divinities]].

{{AFC comment|1=Note: This draft started from a complete copy of [[Onmyōji]] as it has a lot of redlinks with claims I want to keep. I will trim down into just the claim on an individual thing later[[User:Immanuelle|'''Immanuel'''le]] ❤️💚💙 [[User_talk:Immanuelle|(talk to the cutest Wikipedian)]] 01:41, 25 April 2023 (UTC)}} {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} (Rōkoku Hakase, 漏刻博士) is position in the [[Ministry of the Center]] the chief timekeeper.<ref name="titsingh427">Titsingh, Isaac. (1834). {{Google books|18oNAAAAIAAJ|''Annales des empereurs du japon,'' p. 427.|page=427}}</ref><ref>https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/10.7916/d8-3zya-0s65/download</ref><ref>https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/10.7916/D8HD82PN/download</ref><ref>https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/id=8943</ref><ref>https://bazhum.muzhp.pl/media/files/Analecta_Nipponica/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1-s139-202/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1-s139-202.pdf</ref>
The position was a {{ill|Hakase|ja|博士 (文官)}} under the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制}} within the {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}}. The {{ill|Japanese reading|ja|和訓}} (和訓) for this position was "Tokitsukasa" (ときつかさ), while its {{ill|Chinese name|ja|唐名}} was "Shijin" (司辰) or "Keiko-shi" (契壷司). Two individuals typically filled this role, though additional deputy officials ({{ill|Gonkan|ja|権官}}) were occasionally appointed. Officially classified as {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Lower Grade|ja|従七位下|1=Junior Seventh Rank|lt=Junior Seventh Rank, Lower Grade|3=従七位}}, individuals of higher ranks, such as the fifth or sixth ranks, were sometimes appointed to this position (as noted in the {{ill|Shokugenshō|ja|職源鈔}}). [[ja:漏刻博士]] The Rōkoku Hakase supervised the {{ill|Morishin-chō|ja|守辰丁}}, a group of 20 individuals selected from {{ill|Shichō|ja|仕丁}}, who guarded the {{ill|Water clocks|ja|漏刻}} and operated them to measure time. At designated times, they would order the Morishin-chō to strike the {{ill|bells|ja|鐘}} located within the Onmyōryō. During the [[Emperor of Japan|Emperor]]'s {{ill|Imperial visits|ja|行幸}}, one Rōkoku Hakase and twelve Morishin-chō were required to accompany the water clock.
In {{ill|Tang dynasty|ja|唐}}, a similar role for a Rōkoku Hakase existed, but the responsibilities were distinct. In Tang China, the practical tasks of water clocks were managed by officials such as Kekkosei (挈壺正), Shijin (司辰), and Rokoku Tenshi (漏刻典事), while the Rōkoku Hakase focused on teaching students of water clocks (Rokokusei). Conversely, in Japan, the practical roles of Kekkosei and related officials were incorporated into the duties of the Rōkoku Hakase. Japan did not establish a Rokokusei system, meaning that Rōkoku Hakase did not have educational duties. This contrasts with the roles of {{ill|Tenmon Hakase|ja|天文博士}} (Astronomy Doctor) and {{ill|Reki Hakase|ja|暦博士}} (Calendar Doctor), who both managed practical tasks and taught students.<ref>Masashi Kinoshita, ''Kodai no Rōkoku to Jikoku Seido'' (Ancient Water Clocks and Time Systems), Yoshikawa Kōbunkan, 2020, ISBN 978-4-642-04657-2, pp. 307–312.</ref>
The water clock system appears to have declined relatively early. By the {{ill|Insei|ja|院政}} period, the role of Rōkoku Hakase became symbolic, primarily awarded to members of the {{ill|Kamo clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} or {{ill|Abe clan|ja|阿倍氏}} or their recommended disciples. Figures such as {{ill|Sugano no Suketaka|ja|菅野季親}} and {{ill|Sugano no Suketaka|ja|菅野季長}} became Rōkoku Hakase not for expertise in water clocks but for their skill in annual divination ({{ill|Nensei|ja|年筮}}). Although water clocks were also installed in {{ill|Dazaifu|ja|大宰府}} and {{ill|Mutsu Province|ja|陸奥国}} (and later in {{ill|Dewa Province|ja|出羽国}}), they were managed solely by Morishin-chō without a corresponding Hakase.
== History == Later, [[Emperor Tenmu]] was such a master of astrology and fugue that he took his own divination tools and told fortunes during the [[Jinshin War]]. He also had a deep knowledge of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy, which led to the establishment of the Bureau of Onmyō and Japan's first [[observatory]] in 676, and the use of the term "onmyōji" in 685, which further increased the popularity of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy. In 718, the [[Yōrō Code]] established the Bureau of Onmyō as an internal department of the Ministry of Center, and when it was stipulated that the positions of {{ill|Temmon Hakase|lt=Doctor of Astrology|ja|天文博士}}, {{ill|Onmyō Hakase|lt=Doctor of Onmyō|ja|陰陽博士}}, onmyōji, {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}}, and {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} should be permanently assigned as technical officers, the Bureau of Onmyō became officially in charge of divination along with the [[turtle shell]] diviners who belonged to the [[Department of Divinities]].
== Related Articles == * {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制}} * {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}} * {{ill|Water clock|ja|漏刻}}

{{AFC comment|1=Note: This draft started from a complete copy of [[Onmyōji]] as it has a lot of redlinks with claims I want to keep. I will trim down into just the claim on an individual thing later[[User:Immanuelle|'''Immanuel'''le]] ❤️💚💙 [[User_talk:Immanuelle|(talk to the cutest Wikipedian)]] 01:41, 25 April 2023 (UTC)}} {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} (Rōkoku Hakase, 漏刻博士) is position in the [[Ministry of the Center]] the chief timekeeper.<ref name="titsingh427">Titsingh, Isaac. (1834). {{Google books|18oNAAAAIAAJ|''Annales des empereurs du japon,'' p. 427.|page=427}}</ref><ref>https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/10.7916/d8-3zya-0s65/download</ref><ref>https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/10.7916/D8HD82PN/download</ref><ref>https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/id=8943</ref><ref>https://bazhum.muzhp.pl/media/files/Analecta_Nipponica/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1-s139-202/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1-s139-202.pdf</ref>
The position was a {{ill|Hakase|ja|博士 (文官)}} under the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制}} within the {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}}. The {{ill|Japanese reading|ja|和訓}} (和訓) for this position was "Tokitsukasa" (ときつかさ), while its {{ill|Chinese name|ja|唐名}} was "Shijin" (司辰) or "Keiko-shi" (契壷司). Two individuals typically filled this role, though additional deputy officials ({{ill|Gonkan|ja|権官}}) were occasionally appointed. Officially classified as {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Lower Grade|ja|従七位下|1=Junior Seventh Rank|lt=Junior Seventh Rank, Lower Grade|3=従七位}}, individuals of higher ranks, such as the fifth or sixth ranks, were sometimes appointed to this position (as noted in the {{ill|Shokugenshō|ja|職源鈔}}). [[ja:漏刻博士]] The Rōkoku Hakase supervised the {{ill|Morishin-chō|ja|守辰丁}}, a group of 20 individuals selected from {{ill|Shichō|ja|仕丁}}, who guarded the {{ill|Water clocks|ja|漏刻}} and operated them to measure time. At designated times, they would order the Morishin-chō to strike the {{ill|bells|ja|鐘}} located within the Onmyōryō. During the [[Emperor of Japan|Emperor]]'s {{ill|Imperial visits|ja|行幸}}, one Rōkoku Hakase and twelve Morishin-chō were required to accompany the water clock.
In {{ill|Tang dynasty|ja|唐}}, a similar role for a Rōkoku Hakase existed, but the responsibilities were distinct. In Tang China, the practical tasks of water clocks were managed by officials such as Kekkosei (挈壺正), Shijin (司辰), and Rokoku Tenshi (漏刻典事), while the Rōkoku Hakase focused on teaching students of water clocks (Rokokusei). Conversely, in Japan, the practical roles of Kekkosei and related officials were incorporated into the duties of the Rōkoku Hakase. Japan did not establish a Rokokusei system, meaning that Rōkoku Hakase did not have educational duties. This contrasts with the roles of {{ill|Tenmon Hakase|ja|天文博士}} (Astronomy Doctor) and {{ill|Reki Hakase|ja|暦博士}} (Calendar Doctor), who both managed practical tasks and taught students.<ref>Masashi Kinoshita, ''Kodai no Rōkoku to Jikoku Seido'' (Ancient Water Clocks and Time Systems), Yoshikawa Kōbunkan, 2020, ISBN 978-4-642-04657-2, pp. 307–312.</ref>
The water clock system appears to have declined relatively early. By the {{ill|Insei|ja|院政}} period, the role of Rōkoku Hakase became symbolic, primarily awarded to members of the {{ill|Kamo clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} or {{ill|Abe clan|ja|阿倍氏}} or their recommended disciples. Figures such as {{ill|Sugano no Suketaka|ja|菅野季親}} and {{ill|Sugano no Suketaka|ja|菅野季長}} became Rōkoku Hakase not for expertise in water clocks but for their skill in annual divination ({{ill|Nensei|ja|年筮}}). Although water clocks were also installed in {{ill|Dazaifu|ja|大宰府}} and {{ill|Mutsu Province|ja|陸奥国}} (and later in {{ill|Dewa Province|ja|出羽国}}), they were managed solely by Morishin-chō without a corresponding Hakase.
== History == Later, [[Emperor Tenmu]] was such a master of astrology and fugue that he took his own divination tools and told fortunes during the [[Jinshin War]]. He also had a deep knowledge of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy, which led to the establishment of the Bureau of Onmyō and Japan's first [[observatory]] in 676, and the use of the term "onmyōji" in 685, which further increased the popularity of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy. In 718, the [[Yōrō Code]] established the Bureau of Onmyō as an internal department of the Ministry of Center, and when it was stipulated that the positions of {{ill|Temmon Hakase|lt=Doctor of Astrology|ja|天文博士}}, {{ill|Onmyō Hakase|lt=Doctor of Onmyō|ja|陰陽博士}}, onmyōji, {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}}, and {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} should be permanently assigned as technical officers, the Bureau of Onmyō became officially in charge of divination along with the [[turtle shell]] diviners who belonged to the [[Department of Divinities]].

{{AFC comment|1=Note: This draft started from a complete copy of [[Onmyōji]] as it has a lot of redlinks with claims I want to keep. I will trim down into just the claim on an individual thing later[[User:Immanuelle|'''Immanuel'''le]] ❤️💚💙 [[User_talk:Immanuelle|(talk to the cutest Wikipedian)]] 01:41, 25 April 2023 (UTC)}} {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} (Rōkoku Hakase, 漏刻博士) is position in the [[Ministry of the Center]] the chief timekeeper.<ref name="titsingh427">Titsingh, Isaac. (1834). {{Google books|18oNAAAAIAAJ|''Annales des empereurs du japon,'' p. 427.|page=427}}</ref><ref>https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/10.7916/d8-3zya-0s65/download</ref><ref>https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/10.7916/D8HD82PN/download</ref><ref>https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/id=8943</ref><ref>https://bazhum.muzhp.pl/media/files/Analecta_Nipponica/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1-s139-202/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1-s139-202.pdf</ref>
The position was a {{ill|Hakase|ja|博士 (文官)}} under the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制}} within the {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}}. The {{ill|Japanese reading|ja|和訓}} (和訓) for this position was "Tokitsukasa" (ときつかさ), while its {{ill|Chinese name|ja|唐名}} was "Shijin" (司辰) or "Keiko-shi" (契壷司). Two individuals typically filled this role, though additional deputy officials ({{ill|Gonkan|ja|権官}}) were occasionally appointed. Officially classified as {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Lower Grade|ja|従七位下|1=Junior Seventh Rank|lt=Junior Seventh Rank, Lower Grade|3=従七位}}, individuals of higher ranks, such as the fifth or sixth ranks, were sometimes appointed to this position (as noted in the {{ill|Shokugenshō|ja|職源鈔}}). [[ja:漏刻博士]] The Rōkoku Hakase supervised the {{ill|Morishin-chō|ja|守辰丁}}, a group of 20 individuals selected from {{ill|Shichō|ja|仕丁}}, who guarded the {{ill|Water clocks|ja|漏刻}} and operated them to measure time. At designated times, they would order the Morishin-chō to strike the {{ill|bells|ja|鐘}} located within the Onmyōryō. During the [[Emperor of Japan|Emperor]]'s {{ill|Imperial visits|ja|行幸}}, one Rōkoku Hakase and twelve Morishin-chō were required to accompany the water clock.
In {{ill|Tang dynasty|ja|唐}}, a similar role for a Rōkoku Hakase existed, but the responsibilities were distinct. In Tang China, the practical tasks of water clocks were managed by officials such as Kekkosei (挈壺正), Shijin (司辰), and Rokoku Tenshi (漏刻典事), while the Rōkoku Hakase focused on teaching students of water clocks (Rokokusei). Conversely, in Japan, the practical roles of Kekkosei and related officials were incorporated into the duties of the Rōkoku Hakase. Japan did not establish a Rokokusei system, meaning that Rōkoku Hakase did not have educational duties. This contrasts with the roles of {{ill|Tenmon Hakase|ja|天文博士}} (Astronomy Doctor) and {{ill|Reki Hakase|ja|暦博士}} (Calendar Doctor), who both managed practical tasks and taught students.<ref>Masashi Kinoshita, ''Kodai no Rōkoku to Jikoku Seido'' (Ancient Water Clocks and Time Systems), Yoshikawa Kōbunkan, 2020, ISBN 978-4-642-04657-2, pp. 307–312.</ref>
The water clock system appears to have declined relatively early. By the {{ill|Insei|ja|院政}} period, the role of Rōkoku Hakase became symbolic, primarily awarded to members of the {{ill|Kamo clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} or {{ill|Abe clan|ja|阿倍氏}} or their recommended disciples. Figures such as {{ill|Sugano no Suketaka|ja|菅野季親}} and {{ill|Sugano no Suketaka|ja|菅野季長}} became Rōkoku Hakase not for expertise in water clocks but for their skill in annual divination ({{ill|Nensei|ja|年筮}}). Although water clocks were also installed in {{ill|Dazaifu|ja|大宰府}} and {{ill|Mutsu Province|ja|陸奥国}} (and later in {{ill|Dewa Province|ja|出羽国}}), they were managed solely by Morishin-chō without a corresponding Hakase.
== History == Later, [[Emperor Tenmu]] was such a master of astrology and fugue that he took his own divination tools and told fortunes during the [[Jinshin War]]. He also had a deep knowledge of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy, which led to the establishment of the Bureau of Onmyō and Japan's first [[observatory]] in 676, and the use of the term "onmyōji" in 685, which further increased the popularity of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy. In 718, the [[Yōrō Code]] established the Bureau of Onmyō as an internal department of the Ministry of Center, and when it was stipulated that the positions of {{ill|Temmon Hakase|lt=Doctor of Astrology|ja|天文博士}}, {{ill|Onmyō Hakase|lt=Doctor of Onmyō|ja|陰陽博士}}, onmyōji, {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}}, and {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} should be permanently assigned as technical officers, the Bureau of Onmyō became officially in charge of divination along with the [[turtle shell]] diviners who belonged to the [[Department of Divinities]].

{{AFC comment|1=Note: This draft started from a complete copy of [[Onmyōji]] as it has a lot of redlinks with claims I want to keep. I will trim down into just the claim on an individual thing later[[User:Immanuelle|'''Immanuel'''le]] ❤️💚💙 [[User_talk:Immanuelle|(talk to the cutest Wikipedian)]] 01:41, 25 April 2023 (UTC)}} {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} (Rōkoku Hakase, 漏刻博士) is position in the [[Ministry of the Center]] the chief timekeeper.<ref name="titsingh427">Titsingh, Isaac. (1834). {{Google books|18oNAAAAIAAJ|''Annales des empereurs du japon,'' p. 427.|page=427}}</ref><ref>https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/10.7916/d8-3zya-0s65/download</ref><ref>https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/10.7916/D8HD82PN/download</ref><ref>https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/id=8943</ref><ref>https://bazhum.muzhp.pl/media/files/Analecta_Nipponica/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1-s139-202/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1-s139-202.pdf</ref>
The position was a {{ill|Hakase|ja|博士 (文官)}} under the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制}} within the {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}}. The {{ill|Japanese reading|ja|和訓}} (和訓) for this position was "Tokitsukasa" (ときつかさ), while its {{ill|Chinese name|ja|唐名}} was "Shijin" (司辰) or "Keiko-shi" (契壷司). Two individuals typically filled this role, though additional deputy officials ({{ill|Gonkan|ja|権官}}) were occasionally appointed. Officially classified as {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Lower Grade|ja|従七位下|1=Junior Seventh Rank|lt=Junior Seventh Rank, Lower Grade|3=従七位}}, individuals of higher ranks, such as the fifth or sixth ranks, were sometimes appointed to this position (as noted in the {{ill|Shokugenshō|ja|職源鈔}}). [[ja:漏刻博士]] The Rōkoku Hakase supervised the {{ill|Morishin-chō|ja|守辰丁}}, a group of 20 individuals selected from {{ill|Shichō|ja|仕丁}}, who guarded the {{ill|Water clocks|ja|漏刻}} and operated them to measure time. At designated times, they would order the Morishin-chō to strike the {{ill|bells|ja|鐘}} located within the Onmyōryō. During the [[Emperor of Japan|Emperor]]'s {{ill|Imperial visits|ja|行幸}}, one Rōkoku Hakase and twelve Morishin-chō were required to accompany the water clock.
In {{ill|Tang dynasty|ja|唐}}, a similar role for a Rōkoku Hakase existed, but the responsibilities were distinct. In Tang China, the practical tasks of water clocks were managed by officials such as Kekkosei (挈壺正), Shijin (司辰), and Rokoku Tenshi (漏刻典事), while the Rōkoku Hakase focused on teaching students of water clocks (Rokokusei). Conversely, in Japan, the practical roles of Kekkosei and related officials were incorporated into the duties of the Rōkoku Hakase. Japan did not establish a Rokokusei system, meaning that Rōkoku Hakase did not have educational duties. This contrasts with the roles of {{ill|Tenmon Hakase|ja|天文博士}} (Astronomy Doctor) and {{ill|Reki Hakase|ja|暦博士}} (Calendar Doctor), who both managed practical tasks and taught students.<ref>Masashi Kinoshita, ''Kodai no Rōkoku to Jikoku Seido'' (Ancient Water Clocks and Time Systems), Yoshikawa Kōbunkan, 2020, ISBN 978-4-642-04657-2, pp. 307–312.</ref>
The water clock system appears to have declined relatively early. By the {{ill|Insei|ja|院政}} period, the role of Rōkoku Hakase became symbolic, primarily awarded to members of the {{ill|Kamo clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} or {{ill|Abe clan|ja|阿倍氏}} or their recommended disciples. Figures such as {{ill|Sugano no Suketaka|ja|菅野季親}} and {{ill|Sugano no Suketaka|ja|菅野季長}} became Rōkoku Hakase not for expertise in water clocks but for their skill in annual divination ({{ill|Nensei|ja|年筮}}). Although water clocks were also installed in {{ill|Dazaifu|ja|大宰府}} and {{ill|Mutsu Province|ja|陸奥国}} (and later in {{ill|Dewa Province|ja|出羽国}}), they were managed solely by Morishin-chō without a corresponding Hakase.
== History == Later, [[Emperor Tenmu]] was such a master of astrology and fugue that he took his own divination tools and told fortunes during the [[Jinshin War]]. He also had a deep knowledge of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy, which led to the establishment of the Bureau of Onmyō and Japan's first [[observatory]] in 676, and the use of the term "onmyōji" in 685, which further increased the popularity of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy. In 718, the [[Yōrō Code]] established the Bureau of Onmyō as an internal department of the Ministry of Center, and when it was stipulated that the positions of {{ill|Temmon Hakase|lt=Doctor of Astrology|ja|天文博士}}, {{ill|Onmyō Hakase|lt=Doctor of Onmyō|ja|陰陽博士}}, onmyōji, {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}}, and {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} should be permanently assigned as technical officers, the Bureau of Onmyō became officially in charge of divination along with the [[turtle shell]] diviners who belonged to the [[Department of Divinities]].

The position was a {{ill|Hakase|ja|博士 (文官)}} under the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制}} within the {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}}. The {{ill|Japanese reading|ja|和訓}} (和訓) for this position was "Tokitsukasa" (ときつかさ), while its {{ill|Chinese name|ja|唐名}} was "Shijin" (司辰) or "Keiko-shi" (契壷司). Two individuals typically filled this role, though additional deputy officials ({{ill|Gonkan|ja|権官}}) were occasionally appointed. Officially classified as {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Lower Grade|ja|従七位下|1=Junior Seventh Rank|lt=Junior Seventh Rank, Lower Grade|3=従七位}}, individuals of higher ranks, such as the fifth or sixth ranks, were sometimes appointed to this position (as noted in the {{ill|Shokugenshō|ja|職源鈔}}). [[ja:漏刻博士]] The Rōkoku Hakase supervised the {{ill|Morishin-chō|ja|守辰丁}}, a group of 20 individuals selected from {{ill|Shichō|ja|仕丁}}, who guarded the {{ill|Water clocks|ja|漏刻}} and operated them to measure time. At designated times, they would order the Morishin-chō to strike the {{ill|bells|ja|鐘}} located within the Onmyōryō. During the [[Emperor of Japan|Emperor]]'s {{ill|Imperial visits|ja|行幸}}, one Rōkoku Hakase and twelve Morishin-chō were required to accompany the water clock.
In {{ill|Tang dynasty|ja|唐}}, a similar role for a Rōkoku Hakase existed, but the responsibilities were distinct. In Tang China, the practical tasks of water clocks were managed by officials such as Kekkosei (挈壺正), Shijin (司辰), and Rokoku Tenshi (漏刻典事), while the Rōkoku Hakase focused on teaching students of water clocks (Rokokusei). Conversely, in Japan, the practical roles of Kekkosei and related officials were incorporated into the duties of the Rōkoku Hakase. Japan did not establish a Rokokusei system, meaning that Rōkoku Hakase did not have educational duties. This contrasts with the roles of {{ill|Tenmon Hakase|ja|天文博士}} (Astronomy Doctor) and {{ill|Reki Hakase|ja|暦博士}} (Calendar Doctor), who both managed practical tasks and taught students.<ref>Masashi Kinoshita, ''Kodai no Rōkoku to Jikoku Seido'' (Ancient Water Clocks and Time Systems), Yoshikawa Kōbunkan, 2020, ISBN 978-4-642-04657-2, pp. 307–312.</ref>
The water clock system appears to have declined relatively early. By the {{ill|Insei|ja|院政}} period, the role of Rōkoku Hakase became symbolic, primarily awarded to members of the {{ill|Kamo clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} or {{ill|Abe clan|ja|阿倍氏}} or their recommended disciples. Figures such as {{ill|Sugano no Suketaka|ja|菅野季親}} and {{ill|Sugano no Suketaka|ja|菅野季長}} became Rōkoku Hakase not for expertise in water clocks but for their skill in annual divination ({{ill|Nensei|ja|年筮}}). Although water clocks were also installed in {{ill|Dazaifu|ja|大宰府}} and {{ill|Mutsu Province|ja|陸奥国}} (and later in {{ill|Dewa Province|ja|出羽国}}), they were managed solely by Morishin-chō without a corresponding Hakase.
== History == Later, [[Emperor Tenmu]] was such a master of astrology and fugue that he took his own divination tools and told fortunes during the [[Jinshin War]]. He also had a deep knowledge of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy, which led to the establishment of the Bureau of Onmyō and Japan's first [[observatory]] in 676, and the use of the term "onmyōji" in 685, which further increased the popularity of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy. In 718, the [[Yōrō Code]] established the Bureau of Onmyō as an internal department of the Ministry of Center, and when it was stipulated that the positions of {{ill|Temmon Hakase|lt=Doctor of Astrology|ja|天文博士}}, {{ill|Onmyō Hakase|lt=Doctor of Onmyō|ja|陰陽博士}}, onmyōji, {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}}, and {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} should be permanently assigned as technical officers, the Bureau of Onmyō became officially in charge of divination along with the [[turtle shell]] diviners who belonged to the [[Department of Divinities]].

The {{ill|Japanese reading|ja|和訓}} (和訓) for this position was "Tokitsukasa" (ときつかさ), while its {{ill|Chinese name|ja|唐名}} was "Shijin" (司辰) or "Keiko-shi" (契壷司). Two individuals typically filled this role, though additional deputy officials ({{ill|Gonkan|ja|権官}}) were occasionally appointed. Officially classified as {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Lower Grade|ja|従七位下|1=Junior Seventh Rank|lt=Junior Seventh Rank, Lower Grade|3=従七位}}, individuals of higher ranks, such as the fifth or sixth ranks, were sometimes appointed to this position (as noted in the {{ill|Shokugenshō|ja|職源鈔}}). [[ja:漏刻博士]] The Rōkoku Hakase supervised the {{ill|Morishin-chō|ja|守辰丁}}, a group of 20 individuals selected from {{ill|Shichō|ja|仕丁}}, who guarded the {{ill|Water clocks|ja|漏刻}} and operated them to measure time. At designated times, they would order the Morishin-chō to strike the {{ill|bells|ja|鐘}} located within the Onmyōryō. During the [[Emperor of Japan|Emperor]]'s {{ill|Imperial visits|ja|行幸}}, one Rōkoku Hakase and twelve Morishin-chō were required to accompany the water clock.
In {{ill|Tang dynasty|ja|唐}}, a similar role for a Rōkoku Hakase existed, but the responsibilities were distinct. In Tang China, the practical tasks of water clocks were managed by officials such as Kekkosei (挈壺正), Shijin (司辰), and Rokoku Tenshi (漏刻典事), while the Rōkoku Hakase focused on teaching students of water clocks (Rokokusei). Conversely, in Japan, the practical roles of Kekkosei and related officials were incorporated into the duties of the Rōkoku Hakase. Japan did not establish a Rokokusei system, meaning that Rōkoku Hakase did not have educational duties. This contrasts with the roles of {{ill|Tenmon Hakase|ja|天文博士}} (Astronomy Doctor) and {{ill|Reki Hakase|ja|暦博士}} (Calendar Doctor), who both managed practical tasks and taught students.<ref>Masashi Kinoshita, ''Kodai no Rōkoku to Jikoku Seido'' (Ancient Water Clocks and Time Systems), Yoshikawa Kōbunkan, 2020, ISBN 978-4-642-04657-2, pp. 307–312.</ref>
The water clock system appears to have declined relatively early. By the {{ill|Insei|ja|院政}} period, the role of Rōkoku Hakase became symbolic, primarily awarded to members of the {{ill|Kamo clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} or {{ill|Abe clan|ja|阿倍氏}} or their recommended disciples. Figures such as {{ill|Sugano no Suketaka|ja|菅野季親}} and {{ill|Sugano no Suketaka|ja|菅野季長}} became Rōkoku Hakase not for expertise in water clocks but for their skill in annual divination ({{ill|Nensei|ja|年筮}}). Although water clocks were also installed in {{ill|Dazaifu|ja|大宰府}} and {{ill|Mutsu Province|ja|陸奥国}} (and later in {{ill|Dewa Province|ja|出羽国}}), they were managed solely by Morishin-chō without a corresponding Hakase.
== History == Later, [[Emperor Tenmu]] was such a master of astrology and fugue that he took his own divination tools and told fortunes during the [[Jinshin War]]. He also had a deep knowledge of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy, which led to the establishment of the Bureau of Onmyō and Japan's first [[observatory]] in 676, and the use of the term "onmyōji" in 685, which further increased the popularity of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy. In 718, the [[Yōrō Code]] established the Bureau of Onmyō as an internal department of the Ministry of Center, and when it was stipulated that the positions of {{ill|Temmon Hakase|lt=Doctor of Astrology|ja|天文博士}}, {{ill|Onmyō Hakase|lt=Doctor of Onmyō|ja|陰陽博士}}, onmyōji, {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}}, and {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} should be permanently assigned as technical officers, the Bureau of Onmyō became officially in charge of divination along with the [[turtle shell]] diviners who belonged to the [[Department of Divinities]].

(1834). {{Google books|18oNAAAAIAAJ|''Annales des empereurs du japon,'' p. 427.|page=427}}</ref><ref>https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/10.7916/d8-3zya-0s65/download</ref><ref>https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/10.7916/D8HD82PN/download</ref><ref>https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/id=8943</ref><ref>https://bazhum.muzhp.pl/media/files/Analecta_Nipponica/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1-s139-202/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1-s139-202.pdf</ref>
The position was a {{ill|Hakase|ja|博士 (文官)}} under the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制}} within the {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}}. The {{ill|Japanese reading|ja|和訓}} (和訓) for this position was "Tokitsukasa" (ときつかさ), while its {{ill|Chinese name|ja|唐名}} was "Shijin" (司辰) or "Keiko-shi" (契壷司). Two individuals typically filled this role, though additional deputy officials ({{ill|Gonkan|ja|権官}}) were occasionally appointed. Officially classified as {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Lower Grade|ja|従七位下|1=Junior Seventh Rank|lt=Junior Seventh Rank, Lower Grade|3=従七位|1=Junior Seventh Rank}}, individuals of higher ranks, such as the fifth or sixth ranks, were sometimes appointed to this position (as noted in the {{ill|Shokugenshō|ja|職源鈔}}). [[ja:漏刻博士]] The Rōkoku Hakase supervised the {{ill|Morishin-chō|ja|守辰丁}}, a group of 20 individuals selected from {{ill|Shichō|ja|仕丁}}, who guarded the {{ill|Water clocks|ja|漏刻}} and operated them to measure time. At designated times, they would order the Morishin-chō to strike the {{ill|bells|ja|鐘}} located within the Onmyōryō. During the [[Emperor of Japan|Emperor]]'s {{ill|Imperial visits|ja|行幸}}, one Rōkoku Hakase and twelve Morishin-chō were required to accompany the water clock.
In {{ill|Tang dynasty|ja|唐}}, a similar role for a Rōkoku Hakase existed, but the responsibilities were distinct. In Tang China, the practical tasks of water clocks were managed by officials such as Kekkosei (挈壺正), Shijin (司辰), and Rokoku Tenshi (漏刻典事), while the Rōkoku Hakase focused on teaching students of water clocks (Rokokusei). Conversely, in Japan, the practical roles of Kekkosei and related officials were incorporated into the duties of the Rōkoku Hakase. Japan did not establish a Rokokusei system, meaning that Rōkoku Hakase did not have educational duties. This contrasts with the roles of {{ill|Tenmon Hakase|ja|天文博士}} (Astronomy Doctor) and {{ill|Reki Hakase|ja|暦博士}} (Calendar Doctor), who both managed practical tasks and taught students.<ref>Masashi Kinoshita, ''Kodai no Rōkoku to Jikoku Seido'' (Ancient Water Clocks and Time Systems), Yoshikawa Kōbunkan, 2020, ISBN 978-4-642-04657-2, pp. 307–312.</ref>
The water clock system appears to have declined relatively early. By the {{ill|Insei|ja|院政}} period, the role of Rōkoku Hakase became symbolic, primarily awarded to members of the {{ill|Kamo clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} or {{ill|Abe clan|ja|阿倍氏}} or their recommended disciples. Figures such as {{ill|Sugano no Suketaka|ja|菅野季親}} and {{ill|Sugano no Suketaka|ja|菅野季長}} became Rōkoku Hakase not for expertise in water clocks but for their skill in annual divination ({{ill|Nensei|ja|年筮}}). Although water clocks were also installed in {{ill|Dazaifu|ja|大宰府}} and {{ill|Mutsu Province|ja|陸奥国}} (and later in {{ill|Dewa Province|ja|出羽国}}), they were managed solely by Morishin-chō without a corresponding Hakase.
== History == Later, [[Emperor Tenmu]] was such a master of astrology and fugue that he took his own divination tools and told fortunes during the [[Jinshin War]]. He also had a deep knowledge of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy, which led to the establishment of the Bureau of Onmyō and Japan's first [[observatory]] in 676, and the use of the term "onmyōji" in 685, which further increased the popularity of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy. In 718, the [[Yōrō Code]] established the Bureau of Onmyō as an internal department of the Ministry of Center, and when it was stipulated that the positions of {{ill|Temmon Hakase|lt=Doctor of Astrology|ja|天文博士}}, {{ill|Onmyō Hakase|lt=Doctor of Onmyō|ja|陰陽博士}}, onmyōji, {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}}, and {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} should be permanently assigned as technical officers, the Bureau of Onmyō became officially in charge of divination along with the [[turtle shell]] diviners who belonged to the [[Department of Divinities]].

{{AFC comment|1=Note: This draft started from a complete copy of [[Onmyōji]] as it has a lot of redlinks with claims I want to keep. I will trim down into just the claim on an individual thing later[[User:Immanuelle|'''Immanuel'''le]] ❤️💚💙 [[User_talk:Immanuelle|(talk to the cutest Wikipedian)]] 01:41, 25 April 2023 (UTC)}} {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} (Rōkoku Hakase, 漏刻博士) is position in the [[Ministry of the Center]] the chief timekeeper.<ref name="titsingh427">Titsingh, Isaac. (1834). {{Google books|18oNAAAAIAAJ|''Annales des empereurs du japon,'' p. 427.|page=427}}</ref><ref>https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/10.7916/d8-3zya-0s65/download</ref><ref>https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/10.7916/D8HD82PN/download</ref><ref>https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/id=8943</ref><ref>https://bazhum.muzhp.pl/media/files/Analecta_Nipponica/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1-s139-202/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1-s139-202.pdf</ref>
The position was a {{ill|Hakase|ja|博士 (文官)}} under the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制}} within the {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}}. The {{ill|Japanese reading|ja|和訓}} (和訓) for this position was "Tokitsukasa" (ときつかさ), while its {{ill|Chinese name|ja|唐名}} was "Shijin" (司辰) or "Keiko-shi" (契壷司). Two individuals typically filled this role, though additional deputy officials ({{ill|Gonkan|ja|権官}}) were occasionally appointed. Officially classified as {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Lower Grade|ja|従七位下|1=Junior Seventh Rank|lt=Junior Seventh Rank, Lower Grade|3=従七位|1=Junior Seventh Rank}}, individuals of higher ranks, such as the fifth or sixth ranks, were sometimes appointed to this position (as noted in the {{ill|Shokugenshō|ja|職源鈔}}). [[ja:漏刻博士]] The Rōkoku Hakase supervised the {{ill|Morishin-chō|ja|守辰丁}}, a group of 20 individuals selected from {{ill|Shichō|ja|仕丁}}, who guarded the {{ill|Water clocks|ja|漏刻}} and operated them to measure time. At designated times, they would order the Morishin-chō to strike the {{ill|bells|ja|鐘}} located within the Onmyōryō. During the [[Emperor of Japan|Emperor]]'s {{ill|Imperial visits|ja|行幸}}, one Rōkoku Hakase and twelve Morishin-chō were required to accompany the water clock.
In {{ill|Tang dynasty|ja|唐}}, a similar role for a Rōkoku Hakase existed, but the responsibilities were distinct. In Tang China, the practical tasks of water clocks were managed by officials such as Kekkosei (挈壺正), Shijin (司辰), and Rokoku Tenshi (漏刻典事), while the Rōkoku Hakase focused on teaching students of water clocks (Rokokusei). Conversely, in Japan, the practical roles of Kekkosei and related officials were incorporated into the duties of the Rōkoku Hakase. Japan did not establish a Rokokusei system, meaning that Rōkoku Hakase did not have educational duties. This contrasts with the roles of {{ill|Tenmon Hakase|ja|天文博士}} (Astronomy Doctor) and {{ill|Reki Hakase|ja|暦博士}} (Calendar Doctor), who both managed practical tasks and taught students.<ref>Masashi Kinoshita, ''Kodai no Rōkoku to Jikoku Seido'' (Ancient Water Clocks and Time Systems), Yoshikawa Kōbunkan, 2020, ISBN 978-4-642-04657-2, pp. 307–312.</ref>
The water clock system appears to have declined relatively early. By the {{ill|Insei|ja|院政}} period, the role of Rōkoku Hakase became symbolic, primarily awarded to members of the {{ill|Kamo clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} or {{ill|Abe clan|ja|阿倍氏}} or their recommended disciples. Figures such as {{ill|Sugano no Suketaka|ja|菅野季親}} and {{ill|Sugano no Suketaka|ja|菅野季長}} became Rōkoku Hakase not for expertise in water clocks but for their skill in annual divination ({{ill|Nensei|ja|年筮}}). Although water clocks were also installed in {{ill|Dazaifu|ja|大宰府}} and {{ill|Mutsu Province|ja|陸奥国}} (and later in {{ill|Dewa Province|ja|出羽国}}), they were managed solely by Morishin-chō without a corresponding Hakase.
== History == Later, [[Emperor Tenmu]] was such a master of astrology and fugue that he took his own divination tools and told fortunes during the [[Jinshin War]]. He also had a deep knowledge of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy, which led to the establishment of the Bureau of Onmyō and Japan's first [[observatory]] in 676, and the use of the term "onmyōji" in 685, which further increased the popularity of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy. In 718, the [[Yōrō Code]] established the Bureau of Onmyō as an internal department of the Ministry of Center, and when it was stipulated that the positions of {{ill|Temmon Hakase|lt=Doctor of Astrology|ja|天文博士}}, {{ill|Onmyō Hakase|lt=Doctor of Onmyō|ja|陰陽博士}}, onmyōji, {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}}, and {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} should be permanently assigned as technical officers, the Bureau of Onmyō became officially in charge of divination along with the [[turtle shell]] diviners who belonged to the [[Department of Divinities]].

{{AFC comment|1=Note: This draft started from a complete copy of [[Onmyōji]] as it has a lot of redlinks with claims I want to keep. I will trim down into just the claim on an individual thing later[[User:Immanuelle|'''Immanuel'''le]] ❤️💚💙 [[User_talk:Immanuelle|(talk to the cutest Wikipedian)]] 01:41, 25 April 2023 (UTC)}} {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} (Rōkoku Hakase, 漏刻博士) is position in the [[Ministry of the Center]] the chief timekeeper.<ref name="titsingh427">Titsingh, Isaac. (1834). {{Google books|18oNAAAAIAAJ|''Annales des empereurs du japon,'' p. 427.|page=427}}</ref><ref>https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/10.7916/d8-3zya-0s65/download</ref><ref>https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/10.7916/D8HD82PN/download</ref><ref>https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/id=8943</ref><ref>https://bazhum.muzhp.pl/media/files/Analecta_Nipponica/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1-s139-202/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1-s139-202.pdf</ref>
The position was a {{ill|Hakase|ja|博士 (文官)}} under the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制}} within the {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}}. The {{ill|Japanese reading|ja|和訓}} (和訓) for this position was "Tokitsukasa" (ときつかさ), while its {{ill|Chinese name|ja|唐名}} was "Shijin" (司辰) or "Keiko-shi" (契壷司). Two individuals typically filled this role, though additional deputy officials ({{ill|Gonkan|ja|権官}}) were occasionally appointed. Officially classified as {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Lower Grade|ja|従七位下|1=Junior Seventh Rank|lt=Junior Seventh Rank, Lower Grade|3=従七位|1=Junior Seventh Rank}}, individuals of higher ranks, such as the fifth or sixth ranks, were sometimes appointed to this position (as noted in the {{ill|Shokugenshō|ja|職源鈔}}). [[ja:漏刻博士]] The Rōkoku Hakase supervised the {{ill|Morishin-chō|ja|守辰丁}}, a group of 20 individuals selected from {{ill|Shichō|ja|仕丁}}, who guarded the {{ill|Water clocks|ja|漏刻}} and operated them to measure time. At designated times, they would order the Morishin-chō to strike the {{ill|bells|ja|鐘}} located within the Onmyōryō. During the [[Emperor of Japan|Emperor]]'s {{ill|Imperial visits|ja|行幸}}, one Rōkoku Hakase and twelve Morishin-chō were required to accompany the water clock.
In {{ill|Tang dynasty|ja|唐}}, a similar role for a Rōkoku Hakase existed, but the responsibilities were distinct. In Tang China, the practical tasks of water clocks were managed by officials such as Kekkosei (挈壺正), Shijin (司辰), and Rokoku Tenshi (漏刻典事), while the Rōkoku Hakase focused on teaching students of water clocks (Rokokusei). Conversely, in Japan, the practical roles of Kekkosei and related officials were incorporated into the duties of the Rōkoku Hakase. Japan did not establish a Rokokusei system, meaning that Rōkoku Hakase did not have educational duties. This contrasts with the roles of {{ill|Tenmon Hakase|ja|天文博士}} (Astronomy Doctor) and {{ill|Reki Hakase|ja|暦博士}} (Calendar Doctor), who both managed practical tasks and taught students.<ref>Masashi Kinoshita, ''Kodai no Rōkoku to Jikoku Seido'' (Ancient Water Clocks and Time Systems), Yoshikawa Kōbunkan, 2020, ISBN 978-4-642-04657-2, pp. 307–312.</ref>
The water clock system appears to have declined relatively early. By the {{ill|Insei|ja|院政}} period, the role of Rōkoku Hakase became symbolic, primarily awarded to members of the {{ill|Kamo clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} or {{ill|Abe clan|ja|阿倍氏}} or their recommended disciples. Figures such as {{ill|Sugano no Suketaka|ja|菅野季親}} and {{ill|Sugano no Suketaka|ja|菅野季長}} became Rōkoku Hakase not for expertise in water clocks but for their skill in annual divination ({{ill|Nensei|ja|年筮}}). Although water clocks were also installed in {{ill|Dazaifu|ja|大宰府}} and {{ill|Mutsu Province|ja|陸奥国}} (and later in {{ill|Dewa Province|ja|出羽国}}), they were managed solely by Morishin-chō without a corresponding Hakase.
== History == Later, [[Emperor Tenmu]] was such a master of astrology and fugue that he took his own divination tools and told fortunes during the [[Jinshin War]]. He also had a deep knowledge of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy, which led to the establishment of the Bureau of Onmyō and Japan's first [[observatory]] in 676, and the use of the term "onmyōji" in 685, which further increased the popularity of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy. In 718, the [[Yōrō Code]] established the Bureau of Onmyō as an internal department of the Ministry of Center, and when it was stipulated that the positions of {{ill|Temmon Hakase|lt=Doctor of Astrology|ja|天文博士}}, {{ill|Onmyō Hakase|lt=Doctor of Onmyō|ja|陰陽博士}}, onmyōji, {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}}, and {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} should be permanently assigned as technical officers, the Bureau of Onmyō became officially in charge of divination along with the [[turtle shell]] diviners who belonged to the [[Department of Divinities]].

View on everybodywiki here [[:every:Rōkoku Hakase|Rōkoku Hakase]]. [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 21:01, 16 February 2025 (UTC)}} {{afc comment|1=This page was originally created by Immanuelle as a wikipedia draft. It was then automatically transferred to everybodywiki and recovered from there. In the future it will be good to import the revisions. Check page history in case this page was moved, since the everybodywiki page may have been under a different title[[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 20:10, 11 February 2025 (UTC)}}
{{AFC comment|1=Note: This draft started from a complete copy of [[Onmyōji]] as it has a lot of redlinks with claims I want to keep. I will trim down into just the claim on an individual thing later[[User:Immanuelle|'''Immanuel'''le]] ❤️💚💙 [[User_talk:Immanuelle|(talk to the cutest Wikipedian)]] 01:41, 25 April 2023 (UTC)}} {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} (Rōkoku Hakase, 漏刻博士) is position in the [[Ministry of the Center]] the chief timekeeper.<ref name="titsingh427">Titsingh, Isaac. (1834). {{Google books|18oNAAAAIAAJ|''Annales des empereurs du japon,'' p. 427.|page=427}}</ref><ref>https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/10.7916/d8-3zya-0s65/download</ref><ref>https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/10.7916/D8HD82PN/download</ref><ref>https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/id=8943</ref><ref>https://bazhum.muzhp.pl/media/files/Analecta_Nipponica/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1-s139-202/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1-s139-202.pdf</ref>
The position was a {{ill|Hakase|ja|博士 (文官)}} under the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制}} within the {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}}. The {{ill|Japanese reading|ja|和訓}} (和訓) for this position was "Tokitsukasa" (ときつかさ), while its {{ill|Chinese name|ja|唐名}} was "Shijin" (司辰) or "Keiko-shi" (契壷司). Two individuals typically filled this role, though additional deputy officials ({{ill|Gonkan|ja|権官}}) were occasionally appointed. Officially classified as {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Lower Grade|ja|従七位下|1=Junior Seventh Rank|lt=Junior Seventh Rank, Lower Grade|3=従七位|1=Junior Seventh Rank}}, individuals of higher ranks, such as the fifth or sixth ranks, were sometimes appointed to this position (as noted in the {{ill|Shokugenshō|ja|職源鈔}}). [[ja:漏刻博士]] The Rōkoku Hakase supervised the {{ill|Morishin-chō|ja|守辰丁}}, a group of 20 individuals selected from {{ill|Shichō|ja|仕丁}}, who guarded the {{ill|Water clocks|ja|漏刻}} and operated them to measure time. At designated times, they would order the Morishin-chō to strike the {{ill|bells|ja|鐘}} located within the Onmyōryō. During the [[Emperor of Japan|Emperor]]'s {{ill|Imperial visits|ja|行幸}}, one Rōkoku Hakase and twelve Morishin-chō were required to accompany the water clock.
In {{ill|Tang dynasty|ja|唐}}, a similar role for a Rōkoku Hakase existed, but the responsibilities were distinct. In Tang China, the practical tasks of water clocks were managed by officials such as Kekkosei (挈壺正), Shijin (司辰), and Rokoku Tenshi (漏刻典事), while the Rōkoku Hakase focused on teaching students of water clocks (Rokokusei). Conversely, in Japan, the practical roles of Kekkosei and related officials were incorporated into the duties of the Rōkoku Hakase. Japan did not establish a Rokokusei system, meaning that Rōkoku Hakase did not have educational duties. This contrasts with the roles of {{ill|Tenmon Hakase|ja|天文博士}} (Astronomy Doctor) and {{ill|Reki Hakase|ja|暦博士}} (Calendar Doctor), who both managed practical tasks and taught students.<ref>Masashi Kinoshita, ''Kodai no Rōkoku to Jikoku Seido'' (Ancient Water Clocks and Time Systems), Yoshikawa Kōbunkan, 2020, ISBN 978-4-642-04657-2, pp. 307–312.</ref>
The water clock system appears to have declined relatively early. By the {{ill|Insei|ja|院政}} period, the role of Rōkoku Hakase became symbolic, primarily awarded to members of the {{ill|Kamo clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} or {{ill|Abe clan|ja|阿倍氏}} or their recommended disciples. Figures such as {{ill|Sugano no Suketaka|ja|菅野季親}} and {{ill|Sugano no Suketaka|ja|菅野季長}} became Rōkoku Hakase not for expertise in water clocks but for their skill in annual divination ({{ill|Nensei|ja|年筮}}). Although water clocks were also installed in {{ill|Dazaifu|ja|大宰府}} and {{ill|Mutsu Province|ja|陸奥国}} (and later in {{ill|Dewa Province|ja|出羽国}}), they were managed solely by Morishin-chō without a corresponding Hakase.
== History == Later, [[Emperor Tenmu]] was such a master of astrology and fugue that he took his own divination tools and told fortunes during the [[Jinshin War]]. He also had a deep knowledge of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy, which led to the establishment of the Bureau of Onmyō and Japan's first [[observatory]] in 676, and the use of the term "onmyōji" in 685, which further increased the popularity of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy. In 718, the [[Yōrō Code]] established the Bureau of Onmyō as an internal department of the Ministry of Center, and when it was stipulated that the positions of {{ill|Temmon Hakase|lt=Doctor of Astrology|ja|天文博士}}, {{ill|Onmyō Hakase|lt=Doctor of Onmyō|ja|陰陽博士}}, onmyōji, {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}}, and {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} should be permanently assigned as technical officers, the Bureau of Onmyō became officially in charge of divination along with the [[turtle shell]] diviners who belonged to the [[Department of Divinities]].

{{AFC comment|1=Note: This draft started from a complete copy of [[Onmyōji]] as it has a lot of redlinks with claims I want to keep. I will trim down into just the claim on an individual thing later[[User:Immanuelle|'''Immanuel'''le]] ❤️💚💙 [[User_talk:Immanuelle|(talk to the cutest Wikipedian)]] 01:41, 25 April 2023 (UTC)}} {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} (Rōkoku Hakase, 漏刻博士) is position in the [[Ministry of the Center]] the chief timekeeper.<ref name="titsingh427">Titsingh, Isaac. (1834). {{Google books|18oNAAAAIAAJ|''Annales des empereurs du japon,'' p. 427.|page=427}}</ref><ref>https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/10.7916/d8-3zya-0s65/download</ref><ref>https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/10.7916/D8HD82PN/download</ref><ref>https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/id=8943</ref><ref>https://bazhum.muzhp.pl/media/files/Analecta_Nipponica/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1-s139-202/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1-s139-202.pdf</ref>
The position was a {{ill|Hakase|ja|博士 (文官)}} under the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制}} within the {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}}. The {{ill|Japanese reading|ja|和訓}} (和訓) for this position was "Tokitsukasa" (ときつかさ), while its {{ill|Chinese name|ja|唐名}} was "Shijin" (司辰) or "Keiko-shi" (契壷司). Two individuals typically filled this role, though additional deputy officials ({{ill|Gonkan|ja|権官}}) were occasionally appointed. Officially classified as {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Lower Grade|ja|従七位下|1=Junior Seventh Rank|lt=Junior Seventh Rank, Lower Grade|3=従七位|1=Junior Seventh Rank}}, individuals of higher ranks, such as the fifth or sixth ranks, were sometimes appointed to this position (as noted in the {{ill|Shokugenshō|ja|職源鈔}}). [[ja:漏刻博士]] The Rōkoku Hakase supervised the {{ill|Morishin-chō|ja|守辰丁}}, a group of 20 individuals selected from {{ill|Shichō|ja|仕丁}}, who guarded the {{ill|Water clocks|ja|漏刻}} and operated them to measure time. At designated times, they would order the Morishin-chō to strike the {{ill|bells|ja|鐘}} located within the Onmyōryō. During the [[Emperor of Japan|Emperor]]'s {{ill|Imperial visits|ja|行幸}}, one Rōkoku Hakase and twelve Morishin-chō were required to accompany the water clock.
In {{ill|Tang dynasty|ja|唐}}, a similar role for a Rōkoku Hakase existed, but the responsibilities were distinct. In Tang China, the practical tasks of water clocks were managed by officials such as Kekkosei (挈壺正), Shijin (司辰), and Rokoku Tenshi (漏刻典事), while the Rōkoku Hakase focused on teaching students of water clocks (Rokokusei). Conversely, in Japan, the practical roles of Kekkosei and related officials were incorporated into the duties of the Rōkoku Hakase. Japan did not establish a Rokokusei system, meaning that Rōkoku Hakase did not have educational duties. This contrasts with the roles of {{ill|Tenmon Hakase|ja|天文博士}} (Astronomy Doctor) and {{ill|Reki Hakase|ja|暦博士}} (Calendar Doctor), who both managed practical tasks and taught students.<ref>Masashi Kinoshita, ''Kodai no Rōkoku to Jikoku Seido'' (Ancient Water Clocks and Time Systems), Yoshikawa Kōbunkan, 2020, ISBN 978-4-642-04657-2, pp. 307–312.</ref>
The water clock system appears to have declined relatively early. By the {{ill|Insei|ja|院政}} period, the role of Rōkoku Hakase became symbolic, primarily awarded to members of the {{ill|Kamo clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} or {{ill|Abe clan|ja|阿倍氏}} or their recommended disciples. Figures such as {{ill|Sugano no Suketaka|ja|菅野季親}} and {{ill|Sugano no Suketaka|ja|菅野季長}} became Rōkoku Hakase not for expertise in water clocks but for their skill in annual divination ({{ill|Nensei|ja|年筮}}). Although water clocks were also installed in {{ill|Dazaifu|ja|大宰府}} and {{ill|Mutsu Province|ja|陸奥国}} (and later in {{ill|Dewa Province|ja|出羽国}}), they were managed solely by Morishin-chō without a corresponding Hakase.
== History == Later, [[Emperor Tenmu]] was such a master of astrology and fugue that he took his own divination tools and told fortunes during the [[Jinshin War]]. He also had a deep knowledge of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy, which led to the establishment of the Bureau of Onmyō and Japan's first [[observatory]] in 676, and the use of the term "onmyōji" in 685, which further increased the popularity of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy. In 718, the [[Yōrō Code]] established the Bureau of Onmyō as an internal department of the Ministry of Center, and when it was stipulated that the positions of {{ill|Temmon Hakase|lt=Doctor of Astrology|ja|天文博士}}, {{ill|Onmyō Hakase|lt=Doctor of Onmyō|ja|陰陽博士}}, onmyōji, {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}}, and {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} should be permanently assigned as technical officers, the Bureau of Onmyō became officially in charge of divination along with the [[turtle shell]] diviners who belonged to the [[Department of Divinities]].

{{AFC comment|1=Note: This draft started from a complete copy of [[Onmyōji]] as it has a lot of redlinks with claims I want to keep. I will trim down into just the claim on an individual thing later[[User:Immanuelle|'''Immanuel'''le]] ❤️💚💙 [[User_talk:Immanuelle|(talk to the cutest Wikipedian)]] 01:41, 25 April 2023 (UTC)}} {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} (Rōkoku Hakase, 漏刻博士) is position in the [[Ministry of the Center]] the chief timekeeper.<ref name="titsingh427">Titsingh, Isaac. (1834). {{Google books|18oNAAAAIAAJ|''Annales des empereurs du japon,'' p. 427.|page=427}}</ref><ref>https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/10.7916/d8-3zya-0s65/download</ref><ref>https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/10.7916/D8HD82PN/download</ref><ref>https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/id=8943</ref><ref>https://bazhum.muzhp.pl/media/files/Analecta_Nipponica/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1-s139-202/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1-s139-202.pdf</ref>
The position was a {{ill|Hakase|ja|博士 (文官)}} under the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制}} within the {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}}. The {{ill|Japanese reading|ja|和訓}} (和訓) for this position was "Tokitsukasa" (ときつかさ), while its {{ill|Chinese name|ja|唐名}} was "Shijin" (司辰) or "Keiko-shi" (契壷司). Two individuals typically filled this role, though additional deputy officials ({{ill|Gonkan|ja|権官}}) were occasionally appointed. Officially classified as {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Lower Grade|ja|従七位下|1=Junior Seventh Rank|lt=Junior Seventh Rank, Lower Grade|3=従七位|1=Junior Seventh Rank}}, individuals of higher ranks, such as the fifth or sixth ranks, were sometimes appointed to this position (as noted in the {{ill|Shokugenshō|ja|職源鈔}}). [[ja:漏刻博士]] The Rōkoku Hakase supervised the {{ill|Morishin-chō|ja|守辰丁}}, a group of 20 individuals selected from {{ill|Shichō|ja|仕丁}}, who guarded the {{ill|Water clocks|ja|漏刻}} and operated them to measure time. At designated times, they would order the Morishin-chō to strike the {{ill|bells|ja|鐘}} located within the Onmyōryō. During the [[Emperor of Japan|Emperor]]'s {{ill|Imperial visits|ja|行幸}}, one Rōkoku Hakase and twelve Morishin-chō were required to accompany the water clock.
In {{ill|Tang dynasty|ja|唐}}, a similar role for a Rōkoku Hakase existed, but the responsibilities were distinct. In Tang China, the practical tasks of water clocks were managed by officials such as Kekkosei (挈壺正), Shijin (司辰), and Rokoku Tenshi (漏刻典事), while the Rōkoku Hakase focused on teaching students of water clocks (Rokokusei). Conversely, in Japan, the practical roles of Kekkosei and related officials were incorporated into the duties of the Rōkoku Hakase. Japan did not establish a Rokokusei system, meaning that Rōkoku Hakase did not have educational duties. This contrasts with the roles of {{ill|Tenmon Hakase|ja|天文博士}} (Astronomy Doctor) and {{ill|Reki Hakase|ja|暦博士}} (Calendar Doctor), who both managed practical tasks and taught students.<ref>Masashi Kinoshita, ''Kodai no Rōkoku to Jikoku Seido'' (Ancient Water Clocks and Time Systems), Yoshikawa Kōbunkan, 2020, ISBN 978-4-642-04657-2, pp. 307–312.</ref>
The water clock system appears to have declined relatively early. By the {{ill|Insei|ja|院政}} period, the role of Rōkoku Hakase became symbolic, primarily awarded to members of the {{ill|Kamo clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} or {{ill|Abe clan|ja|阿倍氏}} or their recommended disciples. Figures such as {{ill|Sugano no Suketaka|ja|菅野季親}} and {{ill|Sugano no Suketaka|ja|菅野季長}} became Rōkoku Hakase not for expertise in water clocks but for their skill in annual divination ({{ill|Nensei|ja|年筮}}). Although water clocks were also installed in {{ill|Dazaifu|ja|大宰府}} and {{ill|Mutsu Province|ja|陸奥国}} (and later in {{ill|Dewa Province|ja|出羽国}}), they were managed solely by Morishin-chō without a corresponding Hakase.
== History == Later, [[Emperor Tenmu]] was such a master of astrology and fugue that he took his own divination tools and told fortunes during the [[Jinshin War]]. He also had a deep knowledge of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy, which led to the establishment of the Bureau of Onmyō and Japan's first [[observatory]] in 676, and the use of the term "onmyōji" in 685, which further increased the popularity of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy. In 718, the [[Yōrō Code]] established the Bureau of Onmyō as an internal department of the Ministry of Center, and when it was stipulated that the positions of {{ill|Temmon Hakase|lt=Doctor of Astrology|ja|天文博士}}, {{ill|Onmyō Hakase|lt=Doctor of Onmyō|ja|陰陽博士}}, onmyōji, {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}}, and {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} should be permanently assigned as technical officers, the Bureau of Onmyō became officially in charge of divination along with the [[turtle shell]] diviners who belonged to the [[Department of Divinities]].

[[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 21:01, 16 February 2025 (UTC)}} {{afc comment|1=This page was originally created by Immanuelle as a wikipedia draft. It was then automatically transferred to everybodywiki and recovered from there. In the future it will be good to import the revisions. Check page history in case this page was moved, since the everybodywiki page may have been under a different title[[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 20:10, 11 February 2025 (UTC)}}
{{AFC comment|1=Note: This draft started from a complete copy of [[Onmyōji]] as it has a lot of redlinks with claims I want to keep. I will trim down into just the claim on an individual thing later[[User:Immanuelle|'''Immanuel'''le]] ❤️💚💙 [[User_talk:Immanuelle|(talk to the cutest Wikipedian)]] 01:41, 25 April 2023 (UTC)}} {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} (Rōkoku Hakase, 漏刻博士) is position in the [[Ministry of the Center]] the chief timekeeper.<ref name="titsingh427">Titsingh, Isaac. (1834). {{Google books|18oNAAAAIAAJ|''Annales des empereurs du japon,'' p. 427.|page=427}}</ref><ref>https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/10.7916/d8-3zya-0s65/download</ref><ref>https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/10.7916/D8HD82PN/download</ref><ref>https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/id=8943</ref><ref>https://bazhum.muzhp.pl/media/files/Analecta_Nipponica/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1-s139-202/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1-s139-202.pdf</ref>
The position was a {{ill|Hakase|ja|博士 (文官)}} under the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制}} within the {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}}. The {{ill|Japanese reading|ja|和訓}} (和訓) for this position was "Tokitsukasa" (ときつかさ), while its {{ill|Chinese name|ja|唐名}} was "Shijin" (司辰) or "Keiko-shi" (契壷司). Two individuals typically filled this role, though additional deputy officials ({{ill|Gonkan|ja|権官}}) were occasionally appointed. Officially classified as {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Lower Grade|ja|従七位下|1=Junior Seventh Rank|lt=Junior Seventh Rank, Lower Grade|3=従七位|1=Junior Seventh Rank}}, individuals of higher ranks, such as the fifth or sixth ranks, were sometimes appointed to this position (as noted in the {{ill|Shokugenshō|ja|職源鈔}}). [[ja:漏刻博士]] The Rōkoku Hakase supervised the {{ill|Morishin-chō|ja|守辰丁}}, a group of 20 individuals selected from {{ill|Shichō|ja|仕丁}}, who guarded the {{ill|Water clocks|ja|漏刻}} and operated them to measure time. At designated times, they would order the Morishin-chō to strike the {{ill|bells|ja|鐘}} located within the Onmyōryō. During the [[Emperor of Japan|Emperor]]'s {{ill|Imperial visits|ja|行幸}}, one Rōkoku Hakase and twelve Morishin-chō were required to accompany the water clock.
In {{ill|Tang dynasty|ja|唐}}, a similar role for a Rōkoku Hakase existed, but the responsibilities were distinct. In Tang China, the practical tasks of water clocks were managed by officials such as Kekkosei (挈壺正), Shijin (司辰), and Rokoku Tenshi (漏刻典事), while the Rōkoku Hakase focused on teaching students of water clocks (Rokokusei). Conversely, in Japan, the practical roles of Kekkosei and related officials were incorporated into the duties of the Rōkoku Hakase. Japan did not establish a Rokokusei system, meaning that Rōkoku Hakase did not have educational duties. This contrasts with the roles of {{ill|Tenmon Hakase|ja|天文博士}} (Astronomy Doctor) and {{ill|Reki Hakase|ja|暦博士}} (Calendar Doctor), who both managed practical tasks and taught students.<ref>Masashi Kinoshita, ''Kodai no Rōkoku to Jikoku Seido'' (Ancient Water Clocks and Time Systems), Yoshikawa Kōbunkan, 2020, ISBN 978-4-642-04657-2, pp. 307–312.</ref>
The water clock system appears to have declined relatively early. By the {{ill|Insei|ja|院政}} period, the role of Rōkoku Hakase became symbolic, primarily awarded to members of the {{ill|Kamo clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} or {{ill|Abe clan|ja|阿倍氏}} or their recommended disciples. Figures such as {{ill|Sugano no Suketaka|ja|菅野季親}} and {{ill|Sugano no Suketaka|ja|菅野季長}} became Rōkoku Hakase not for expertise in water clocks but for their skill in annual divination ({{ill|Nensei|ja|年筮}}). Although water clocks were also installed in {{ill|Dazaifu|ja|大宰府}} and {{ill|Mutsu Province|ja|陸奥国}} (and later in {{ill|Dewa Province|ja|出羽国}}), they were managed solely by Morishin-chō without a corresponding Hakase.
== History == Later, [[Emperor Tenmu]] was such a master of astrology and fugue that he took his own divination tools and told fortunes during the [[Jinshin War]]. He also had a deep knowledge of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy, which led to the establishment of the Bureau of Onmyō and Japan's first [[observatory]] in 676, and the use of the term "onmyōji" in 685, which further increased the popularity of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy. In 718, the [[Yōrō Code]] established the Bureau of Onmyō as an internal department of the Ministry of Center, and when it was stipulated that the positions of {{ill|Temmon Hakase|lt=Doctor of Astrology|ja|天文博士}}, {{ill|Onmyō Hakase|lt=Doctor of Onmyō|ja|陰陽博士}}, onmyōji, {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}}, and {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} should be permanently assigned as technical officers, the Bureau of Onmyō became officially in charge of divination along with the [[turtle shell]] diviners who belonged to the [[Department of Divinities]].
== Related Articles == * {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制}} * {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}} * {{ill|Water clock|ja|漏刻}}

View on everybodywiki here [[:every:Rōkoku Hakase|Rōkoku Hakase]]. [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 21:01, 16 February 2025 (UTC)}} {{afc comment|1=This page was originally created by Immanuelle as a wikipedia draft. It was then automatically transferred to everybodywiki and recovered from there. In the future it will be good to import the revisions. Check page history in case this page was moved, since the everybodywiki page may have been under a different title[[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 20:10, 11 February 2025 (UTC)}}
{{AFC comment|1=Note: This draft started from a complete copy of [[Onmyōji]] as it has a lot of redlinks with claims I want to keep. I will trim down into just the claim on an individual thing later[[User:Immanuelle|'''Immanuel'''le]] ❤️💚💙 [[User_talk:Immanuelle|(talk to the cutest Wikipedian)]] 01:41, 25 April 2023 (UTC)}} {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} (Rōkoku Hakase, 漏刻博士) is position in the [[Ministry of the Center]] the chief timekeeper.<ref name="titsingh427">Titsingh, Isaac. (1834). {{Google books|18oNAAAAIAAJ|''Annales des empereurs du japon,'' p. 427.|page=427}}</ref><ref>https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/10.7916/d8-3zya-0s65/download</ref><ref>https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/10.7916/D8HD82PN/download</ref><ref>https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/id=8943</ref><ref>https://bazhum.muzhp.pl/media/files/Analecta_Nipponica/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1-s139-202/Analecta_Nipponica-r2011-t1-s139-202.pdf</ref>
The position was a {{ill|Hakase|ja|博士 (文官)}} under the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制}} within the {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}}. The {{ill|Japanese reading|ja|和訓}} (和訓) for this position was "Tokitsukasa" (ときつかさ), while its {{ill|Chinese name|ja|唐名}} was "Shijin" (司辰) or "Keiko-shi" (契壷司). Two individuals typically filled this role, though additional deputy officials ({{ill|Gonkan|ja|権官}}) were occasionally appointed. Officially classified as {{ill|Junior Seventh Rank, Lower Grade|ja|従七位下|1=Junior Seventh Rank|lt=Junior Seventh Rank, Lower Grade|3=従七位|1=Junior Seventh Rank}}, individuals of higher ranks, such as the fifth or sixth ranks, were sometimes appointed to this position (as noted in the {{ill|Shokugenshō|ja|職源鈔}}). [[ja:漏刻博士]] The Rōkoku Hakase supervised the {{ill|Morishin-chō|ja|守辰丁}}, a group of 20 individuals selected from {{ill|Shichō|ja|仕丁}}, who guarded the {{ill|Water clocks|ja|漏刻}} and operated them to measure time. At designated times, they would order the Morishin-chō to strike the {{ill|bells|ja|鐘}} located within the Onmyōryō. During the [[Emperor of Japan|Emperor]]'s {{ill|Imperial visits|ja|行幸}}, one Rōkoku Hakase and twelve Morishin-chō were required to accompany the water clock.
In {{ill|Tang dynasty|ja|唐}}, a similar role for a Rōkoku Hakase existed, but the responsibilities were distinct. In Tang China, the practical tasks of water clocks were managed by officials such as Kekkosei (挈壺正), Shijin (司辰), and Rokoku Tenshi (漏刻典事), while the Rōkoku Hakase focused on teaching students of water clocks (Rokokusei). Conversely, in Japan, the practical roles of Kekkosei and related officials were incorporated into the duties of the Rōkoku Hakase. Japan did not establish a Rokokusei system, meaning that Rōkoku Hakase did not have educational duties. This contrasts with the roles of {{ill|Tenmon Hakase|ja|天文博士}} (Astronomy Doctor) and {{ill|Reki Hakase|ja|暦博士}} (Calendar Doctor), who both managed practical tasks and taught students.<ref>Masashi Kinoshita, ''Kodai no Rōkoku to Jikoku Seido'' (Ancient Water Clocks and Time Systems), Yoshikawa Kōbunkan, 2020, ISBN 978-4-642-04657-2, pp. 307–312.</ref>
The water clock system appears to have declined relatively early. By the {{ill|Insei|ja|院政}} period, the role of Rōkoku Hakase became symbolic, primarily awarded to members of the {{ill|Kamo clan|ja|賀茂朝臣氏}} or {{ill|Abe clan|ja|阿倍氏}} or their recommended disciples. Figures such as {{ill|Sugano no Suketaka|ja|菅野季親}} and {{ill|Sugano no Suketaka|ja|菅野季長}} became Rōkoku Hakase not for expertise in water clocks but for their skill in annual divination ({{ill|Nensei|ja|年筮}}). Although water clocks were also installed in {{ill|Dazaifu|ja|大宰府}} and {{ill|Mutsu Province|ja|陸奥国}} (and later in {{ill|Dewa Province|ja|出羽国}}), they were managed solely by Morishin-chō without a corresponding Hakase.
== History == Later, [[Emperor Tenmu]] was such a master of astrology and fugue that he took his own divination tools and told fortunes during the [[Jinshin War]]. He also had a deep knowledge of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy, which led to the establishment of the Bureau of Onmyō and Japan's first [[observatory]] in 676, and the use of the term "onmyōji" in 685, which further increased the popularity of the yin-and-yang five phases philosophy. In 718, the [[Yōrō Code]] established the Bureau of Onmyō as an internal department of the Ministry of Center, and when it was stipulated that the positions of {{ill|Temmon Hakase|lt=Doctor of Astrology|ja|天文博士}}, {{ill|Onmyō Hakase|lt=Doctor of Onmyō|ja|陰陽博士}}, onmyōji, {{ill|Reki Hakase|lt=Doctor of Calendar|ja|暦博士}}, and {{ill|Rōkoku Hakase|lt=Doctor of Water Clock|ja|漏刻博士}} should be permanently assigned as technical officers, the Bureau of Onmyō became officially in charge of divination along with the [[turtle shell]] diviners who belonged to the [[Department of Divinities]].
== Related Articles == * {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制}} * {{ill|Onmyōryō|ja|陰陽寮}} * {{ill|Water clock|ja|漏刻}}
